title: When horror came to Wangaratta, this is how locals rushed to help
text:
Under sunny skies and armed with a shovel, Helen Haines stood next to a pile of dirt, smiling for the camera.

Joined by senator Michelle Ananda-Rajah, council representatives, and locals, Ms Haines spent some of Monday afternoon in Mansfield for an "official sod-turning" for the Victorian town's BMX pump track and dog park.

"Helen was in high spirits. She was upbeat and positive. She saw me and greeted me with open arms and a big smile on her face and then she planted a big kiss on my cheek," Senator Ananda-Rajah said.

" That was just typical Helen. That's who she is. "

It was all part of a busy day for Ms Haines. At about 2pm the independent MP was back in her car for the drive back north to her office in Wangaratta.

The sun was still shining and it was a beautiful 25 degrees Celsius when she arrived.

It was 3:30pm — school pick-up time — and Wangaratta's main street was busy.

Ms Haines parked outside her office in Murphy Street and went to the boot of her car to unpack.

Her day was far from over. Next up for the member for Indi was a 4pm Zoom interview with the ABC's Patricia Karvelas to talk about the new head of the National Anti-Corruption Commission — a federal body Ms Haines had fought to get established.

She never made it to that interview.

'They just ran to help'

Wangaratta's CBD is four large blocks, bisected in one direction by the wide tree-dotted Murphy Street.

Helen Haines was injured outside her Wangaratta office. (ABC News: Annie Brown)

At the north-eastern end, just before the road leaps the Ovens River, sits Ms Haines's office.

Witnesses say that as Ms Haines stood at the rear of her car outside the office, a white Toyota LandCruiser entered Murphy Street from the river end.

It passed Ms Haines on the opposite of the road, did a U-turn, and then rammed the politician, pinning her against her car.

The LandCruiser reversed, and then hit her again.

Those nearby heard a loud bang and a scream.

Barber Ricky Jefferies ran from his shop to see what was going on.

Wangaratta locals were already rushing to help.

Ricky Jefferies intervened in the attack on Helen Haines.

"I saw amazing members of the Wangaratta community who I know … and they were helping," Mr Jefferies said.

"A lot of people got involved immediately and they didn't even check for danger.

"They just ran to help."

At least one bystander had positioned themself between the car and Ms Haines.

While he would later downplay his role, Mr Jefferies leapt into action.

He dragged the driver from the LandCruiser and leant over him.

He took a knife from the driver's pocket and threw it away.

"Once he was on the ground and he was no longer a threat, I just stood with him and told him that he can't leave," Mr Jefferies said.

And in a true moment of humanity, he told the driver: "Everything is alright, mate. You'll be alright."

"It was the right thing to do and to show him kindness and grace at a time that could have escalated from there," he said.

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has called Mr Jefferies a hero.

Mr Jefferies said he was just "a member of the community" and "a person who had an opportunity to intervene".

Local Cody Lepoidevin also raced to the scene.

"It was quite a horrific scene," Mr Lepoidevin said.

"We knew what needed to happen, whether it was tourniquets, settling the guy down.

" We just had to help Helen as best we could until the ambulance got there. "

He said they sat the driver against a wall.

"[He was] very irrational. He was only concerned about his belongings and his car. His phone, his wallet, and shutting his car door were his main priorities," Mr Lepoidevin said.

"It's quite unsettling."

He said Ms Haines was conscious and stayed remarkably calm and dignified despite her horrific injuries.

"I'm sure if I'd been in Helen's situation there would have been a lot more swear words," Mr Lepoidevin said.

" But she came across lovely … even in that moment. "

A 43-year-old Tarrawingee man, Brendan Nugent, was arrested at the scene.

Ms Haines was flown to hospital for emergency surgery with critical lower leg injuries.

It has been confirmed she has lost one leg, and surgeons at The Alfred are working to save her other one.

On Tuesday people attended a vigil at Wangaratta's Holy Trinity Anglican Cathedral to pray for Helen Haines. (ABC News: Nate Woodall)

A community in shock

In 10 days, Wangaratta will welcome thousands of people to its 36th annual jazz and blues festival.

The event shows off the beauty and hospitality of the city in Victoria's north-east, which sits at the junction of the Ovens and King rivers, nestled on the plains between the Murray and high country.

But whether the people of Wangaratta will feel festive come October 30 remains to be seen.

Right now, it is a community in shock.

"I just can't believe that's happened in Wangaratta," Mayor Irene Grant said.

" It is a safe place and it's a positive place. "

Chris Wernert showed up outside Ms Haines's office with an Australian flag, wearing a T-shirt saying "Wangaratta — this is not us", and calling for respect.

Independent MP for Ovens Valley Steve Manning told ABC Victoria Statewide Mornings Ms Haines had just become a grandmother in recent months.

"This was meant to be a very special time for the Haines family," Mr Manning said.

But he hinted at the dark side that came with a life in politics these days.

"Helen and I spent a couple of hours together at the Wangaratta show only just a couple of weekends ago," he said.

"Helen posted photos of us celebrating what it is that's great about living in our region, and the comments that came to that post were immediately awful.

" On what was meant to be a celebration of regional life, people turned on her and made it into something that it wasn't. "

Visibly distressed locals are laying flowers and letters at the office of Helen Haines.

Less than 24 hours after the shocking attack, Ms Haines's office is surrounded by a sea of flowers and heartfelt notes.

"Thanks for all the wonderful work you have done," one read.

"We are praying for you."

"May you recover quickly and continue to be a light in this world," another read.

Politicians from all sides paid tribute to Ms Haines's tenacity and integrity, and called for the temperature of the public discourse to be lowered.

Senator Ananda-Rajah is "tearing up every five minutes".

"I'm crying. I'm not OK. I'm shattered by this incident," she said.

"Today's been hard. I had a community event this afternoon and I couldn't bring myself to go.

"I just can't face a big crowd. I can't face people right now. I don't know what to say to them. My emotions are too raw."

The police investigation is continuing. Details about Mr Nugent came to light as police raided his home.

Now the 30,000 people of Wangaratta are attempting to come to grips with what has just happened in the town they call home.

title: Contentious hotel development approved for Hobart's eastern shore
text:
A contentious hotel project that has angered community members and divided the local council has been given the green light by Tasmania's planning commission.

Chinese developer Chambroad wants to build the 155-room Kangaroo Bay Hotel at Bellerive on Hobart's eastern shore.

The $65 million project will include accommodation, as well as a range of restaurants and bars, a wellness centre, meeting and function facilities, and new pedestrian and cycleways.

"Our iconic 5-star hotel at Kangaroo Bay will activate the bay and bring jobs and significant economic development to the local area," the company's website says.

A concept image of the Kangaroo Bay development. (Chambroad Australia)

The project was officially declared a major project by the Tasmanian government on October 16, 2024, which meant the proposal needed to be assessed by an independent expert panel appointed by the Tasmanian Planning Commission.

Chambroad project director, Greg Hudson, said the hotel is designed to become a premier tourism and hospitality destination.

"This landmark development will deliver a world-class waterfront destination featuring a 155-room hotel, restaurants, bars, function facilities and publicly accessible open space," he said.

"It will improve foreshore connections from Rosny to Bellerive Village, further strengthening greater Hobart's premium tourism and hospitality offering."

The development will include accommodation, restaurants and bars, a wellness centre, meeting and function facilities and new pedestrian and cycleways, the company says. (Chambroad Australia)

Clarence City Council mayor Brendan Blomeley has previously said the project is the "wrong decision" for the area and the council remains committed to buying the Kangaroo Bay land back.

"We will buy that land back from Chambroad," Mr Blomeley told 936 ABC Hobart Mornings in September last year.

" We'll return it to public ownership and then we'll engage with our community as to what will go there into the future. "

Kangaroo Bay is home to a small marina. (ABC News: Scott Ross)

Mr Hudson said Chambroad Australia has called on the soon-to-be-elected Clarence City councillors to reconsider their litigation by attempting to buy back the land.

"We invite the new councillors to sit down and enter into a constructive dialogue to resolve their litigation and clear the way for construction to commence," he said.

Developers at Chambroad have been trying to get the five-star hotel off the ground since purchasing the land for $2.44 million in 2017.

title: Spirit of Tasmania navigational issue under investigation
text:
TT-Line has launched an investigation after a navigational issue affected one of the Spirit of Tasmania ferries as it approached the Victorian coast last week.

Track maps show Spirit I was heading towards its destination at Geelong in the early hours of Thursday morning when it went off its standard route and made a U-turn close to Point Lonsdale.

This image, from MarineTraffic, shows the Spirit of Tasmania I going off route on the morning of October 15 as it approached Point Lonsdale. (Supplied: MarineTraffic)

"As the vessel was preparing to transit through Port Phillip Heads … the master identified an issue with the ship's navigation equipment," ferry owner TT-Line said in a statement.

"As a precaution, the vessel returned to open water to reset the system before proceeding.

" The reset was successfully completed and the vessel arrived safely at the Port of Geelong, approximately 20 minutes behind schedule. "

The track map also includes Spirit I's route over the past week.

TT-Line is owned by the Tasmanian government.

The company's chief executive Chris Carbone said safety was its "number one priority".

"The company is fully investigating the occurrence and has commenced an independent review to better understand the circumstances," Mr Carbone said.

Spirit of Tasmania testing The Spirit of Tasmania ferry service between Tasmania and the mainland will take no paying passengers for a week in late October as new ships are tested.

"A report was made to the Australian Maritime Safety Authority (AMSA), which is standard practice for incidents of this nature."

It is not yet known whether the navigational issue was related to a technical fault or a human error.

TT-Line said it elected to have a pilot on board the ship the following evening.

The ABC has contacted AMSA for comment.

Old Spirits to be retired

Spirit I and its sister ship Spirit II have been transporting passengers and cargo across Bass Strait since 2002.

Buyer still wanted for Spirit of Tasmania ferries With their final voyage imminent, the future of ferries Spirit I and II is unclear, with no buyer yet and no local berths available to store them.

They will make their final sailings from Devonport to Geelong on Thursday and Friday, respectively.

The ships will be replaced by two new ferries, Spirit IV and Spirit V, which will take their first passengers from October 31.

The Tasmanian government's ferry replacement program has been plagued with cost overruns and infrastructure delays over recent years.

A parliamentary inquiry in May heard the capital program had cost $717 million more than originally expected.

The figure did not include costs associated with berthing both vessels for many months in Scotland and Victoria while their Devonport facility was constructed.

TT-Line is trying to sell the older ferries, but it remains unclear where they will be berthed until a buyer is found.

title: Diamonds boosted by imminent return of vice-captain
text:
Diamonds vice-captain Kate Moloney is on track to return from injury and give Australia a much-needed boost for the Constellation Cup.

Moloney was forced to watch the netball world's number-one side suffer a shock 56–50 loss to the Silver Ferns from the sidelines after a finger laceration in the lead-up to the Auckland series opener.

The Diamonds were already without defender Jo Weston (managed), and the experienced duo were sorely missed against the Commonwealth Games champions.

Diamonds centurions forced to the bench in Constellation Cup loss It was defender Courtney Bruce's 100th milestone game to start the Constellation Cup but the brand new centurion and her captain Liz Watson were both sent to the bench in Australia's 56-50 loss to New Zealand in Auckland.

New Zealand stormed to a 15-goal lead in the first of four matches, forcing Diamonds coach Stacey Marinkovich to bench captain and midcourter Liz Watson alongside goalkeeper Courtney Bruce in her 100th game.

Jamie-Lee Price took over centre duties against New Zealand's Adelaide Lightning star Kate Heffernan, while Jessie Grenvold was tasked with containing Silver Ferns goalscoring superstar Grace Nweke on debut.

Australia cut the deficit to just six goals in the fourth quarter, but the damage had been done.

Georgie Horjus was the only Diamond who remained on the court for four quarters, finishing with a game-high 19 gains and 38 feeds as wing attack.

With the Diamonds set to name their squad this evening, Marinkovich said Melbourne Vixens captain Moloney's return was imminent.

"We'll definitely see her back in the series," Marinkovich said.

"It was a bit of a nasty laceration to her finger, so we had to wait till it pretty much stuck back together.

"It's just one of those innocuous things that happen at training, but she's been able to do all the running and the movement, and yeah, look forward to having her back."

But the midcourt will not be the only area of focus for tomorrow night's game in Christchurch.

Looking to end their five-year drought on Kiwi soil, the Diamonds will need to find a way past the towering defensive duo of Kelly Jackson and Karin Burger.

With goalkeeper Jackson standing at 192cm and goal defence Burger at 184cm, Australia's attacking roster of Kiera Austin, Cara Koenen, Sophie Dwyer and Sophie Garbin struggled to fire.

Marinkovich is urging her Diamonds to start with "immediacy" on the court.

"We were slightly off our pace [in game one], and our numbers would show that we weren't as aggressive as what we needed to be on the ball," she said.

ABC Sport will have live blog coverage of Game II between the Diamonds and Silver Ferns on Wednesday, October 21.

title: Jockeys cleared over Ohope Wins's fatal Caulfield Cup fall
text:
A Racing Victoria investigation into the fall at the Caulfield Cup that resulted in the euthanasia of Ohope Wins has finished, clearing all jockeys involved of any wrongdoing.

Ohope Wins, ridden by Jye McNeil, and Half Yours, ridden by Mark Zahra, both went down in the final straight at the 150th running of the famous 2,400-metre race.

Zahra and Half Yours fell first after getting tangled in the pack chasing eventual winner Kingswood, with Ohope Wins going over the top of the fallen gelding.

Loading...

Last year's Melbourne Cup winner Half Yours suffered superficial cuts and scrapes, but Ohope Wins was assessed on track as having a "serious racing injury" and was put down by on-course veterinarians.

Both jockeys were thrown from their mounts and taken to hospital, delaying the conclusion of the inquiry into the incident, which once again prompted calls for the racing industry to be made more accountable for racehorse deaths.

After hearing evidence from McNeil, Zahra and three other jockeys in the race, Racing Victoria stewards said they "could not attribute the incident to the careless actions of any one particular rider".

The hearing at Racing Victoria headquarters found contact between Kings Valley and Green Spaces with about 300m to go resulted in the latter becoming unbalanced.

Half Yours ran the rest of the course without a rider. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

Green Spaces, ridden by Rachel King, then turned inward and made more contact with apprentice rider Jabez Johnstone's Kings Valley, who also turned inward, resulting in Half Yours being squeezed for room between Kings Valley and Zahrann.

"A short distance later, Half Yours subsequently fell," the stewards' report read.

"Ohope Wins that was trailing was subsequently brought down when unable to avoid the fallen Half Yours."

The incident has been referred to Racing Victoria's Veterinary Services Department, as is standard practice.

Trainer Tony McEvoy said Half Yours was recovering well from injuries and would be rested, while Zahra was meeting with doctors today about a timeline for his return to riding.

McNeil was cleared of any injury and is expected to ride at the Geelong Cup tomorrow.

title: How childlessness grief can reappear later in life
text:
Allison Macaulay-Dear's best friend recently became a grandmother.

"I was thrilled for her obviously," the 62-year-old from South Australia says.

"But it's still painful."

That's because Allison couldn't have children of her own. And it's moments like these when the pain of childlessness feels sharper.

"It just hurts. I haven't got little babies around me and never will. That part is difficult," she says.

Sarah Roberts is a childlessness grief counsellor and lived experience advocate based in Brisbane/Meanjin.

She says while many women adjust to the grief of being childless not by choice over time, living in a culture geared towards families can highlight an "absence of intergenerational relationships".

A timeline of grief

For some childless people, the grief follows a timeline of the baby they never had, says Ms Roberts.

Loving one another through childlessness When IVF didn't work, Susanne and Mike Armour had to face the difficult decision to stop trying for a baby. The couple say their love for one another got them through.

"The child that they are grieving for can age as their peers' children do.

"Loss of a baby, then loss of the school years, then the young adult relationship.

"And then it can be the next generation having their own children."

Allison was only 20 when she had a hysterectomy due to a combination of medical issues. She saw a psychologist at the time who suggested a private writing exercise.

"He said, 'Write a letter to the child you you're never going to have with all the things you would have liked to have done with that child.'

"I [wrote] about me taking them to school for the first time. Those milestones when you're a proud mum.

"I thought it was a good thing, to put those feelings on paper."

The 'pain points' of menopause, retirement and aging

Sarah Roberts says chidlessness grief can follow a timeline of the baby someone never had. (Supplied)

Pain points past the "acute" initial grief of childlessness can happen during perimenopause and menopause, Ms Roberts says.

"We are hit in that sense that 'my biological fertility is really over.'"

During retirement, she says grandchildren can provide someone with a sense of validation — "like a meaningful role they can take on".

"Also that opportunity to just delight in children and have that meaningful relationship without having to necessarily be responsible for them. And it's an added layer of connection to their own children."

That can be quite "tender" for a childless person to witness, Ms Roberts says, for example when approached by friends enthusiastically sharing stories and photos of grandkids.

Aging can bring up fears around not having children to lean on for support, too.

Adult children can provide their parents with physical care, social connection, incidental care — "Help, my TV remote isn't working!" — and advocacy, Ms Roberts says.

"I will often have women downplay their anxieties, saying, 'You can't rely on kids' … but often when the shit hits the fan, kids do step in in some way."

Grief and Loss 24/7 Support Line on 1300 308 307 Bears of Hope (infant loss support for families) on 1300 114 673 We have included a range of helplines here knowing people have many different experiences of childlessness.

Finding meaning and purpose

Ms Roberts is 57 and says she spent a "good decade" grieving not being able to have a child.

These days, she sometimes feels relief.

"When you're in the grief you only grieve for the bits that are lost.

"But I do have little moments that surprise me. Sometimes when I see the challenges parents are experiencing in their lives."

She says it's an ongoing bittersweet experience.

" There are beautiful things I love about my life, but I do have a sense of living with the ongoing absence. "

Finding meaning and purpose outside of having children can help when grief reappears, Ms Roberts says.

"It's a non-conventional life where women have to actively construct meaning and purpose and what that looks like for them.

"I have seen women doing extraordinary things."

The complex label of 'childless not by choice' While childlessness devastates some, not every person who once wanted kids feels crushed when that doesn't eventuate.

For Ms Roberts, that's land regeneration.

"I've found meaning in joining a local bushcare group.

"I also work on my own acreage property in terms of [attracting] native animals."

Building networks with people who aren't parents can be helpful, she says.

"Sometimes even empty-nesters. There is a bit more synergy there and they are also trying to build meaning outside of parenting."

Ms Roberts says every life has highs and lows, and it's finding ways to cope with what that looks like for you.

"While childlessness is challenging, childless women really are capable.

"Particularly when they have had the time and space to make sense of that."

title: Giant tuna puts coastal town in global spotlight after 230kg catch
text:
A team of anglers has become part of a fishing phenomenon that has drawn fishers from across Australia, sent records tumbling and put a small coastal town in Victoria's east in the spotlight.

Off the coast of Lakes Entrance, about 300 kilometres from Melbourne, giant tuna, some weighing more than 200 kilograms, are turning the waters into a fishing hotspot.

Lakes Charter Fishing owner Ricky Grech was among the first to catch one of the giant tuna, landing one weighing 154kg while out fishing with his 10-year-old son Oliver last month.

From there, more anglers continued to reel in record numbers, varying from 140kg to 190kg.

Belinda Brogna recently reeled in a tuna at 204kg at Lakes Entrance. (Supplied: Lakes Charter Fishing)

'Fish of a lifetime'

The largest fish, weighing 231kg, was caught on Sunday by five fishers calling themselves the A Team.

The Gippsland Lakes Fishing Club said the catch was a club record.

"Who's going to bring in the next one?" Mr Grech said.

On shore, car parks were filling with boat trailers and accommodation was in demand.

Tristan Rodgers (right) caught a tuna weighing 217kg. (Supplied: Facebook (Starlo Gets Reel))

Mr Grech said the scale of the activity was unlike anything he had experienced before.

"It's something that I don't think we've really seen so big and phenomenal in Lakes Entrance," he said.

"I think there was well over 150 boats.

"I spoke to one of the fisheries officers and he says it's busier than Easter."

Mr Grech said it was thrilling to hear the record kept getting broken as well.

"I understand it's a fish of a lifetime for some people, so go for it," he said.

Small town spotlight

The influx of anglers has also brought a surge in tourism to Lakes Entrance, with visitors travelling from Sydney, Queensland, Adelaide and Western Australia.

Mr Grech said the flow-on effects were being felt across the town.

"It was unbelievable. [People were] going out for dinner, pizza shops getting booked … Airbnbs and tackle shops being called," he said.

"It all matters for a small regional town."

Victorian Fisheries Authority (VFA) manager of recreational fisheries Taylor Hunt said the town had become a hub for anglers chasing the extraordinary fish.

Fishers have been reeling in large tuna near Lakes Entrance over the past few weeks. (Supplied: Lakes Charter Fishing)

"It's a buzz for the fishing community," Dr Hunt said.

"It's hard to get a car park; there are so many boat trailers there."

Suspected Pacific bluefin catches

The CSIRO just this month confirmed two tuna caught off Western Port Bay in July were Pacific bluefin, the first genetically confirmed fish of the species in Victorian waters.

CSIRO principal research scientist Peter Grewe said further analysis had strengthened confidence in the identification of the two fish.

"I'm extremely confident in these results following a secondary forensic-grade sequencing analysis further confirming our initial quick species ID test," Dr Grewe said.

Researchers are now working to establish whether the monster fish off Lakes Entrance are also Pacific bluefin.

A map illustrating the migration patterns of Pacific bluefin tuna across the Pacific Ocean, including their movements towards Australia and New Zealand. (Supplied: NOAA Fisheries Service)

Dr Grewe said the discovery also highlighted the value of information shared by recreational fishers.

"Information from people out on the water every day is invaluable to scientists," Dr Grewe said.

"Fishers are a wealth of knowledge; they see unusual things, they tell great anecdotes."

Dr Hunt said the suspected Pacific bluefin tuna caught off Lakes Entrance had features that distinguished them from the southern bluefin tuna more commonly caught in Victoria.

"And they look just like Pacific bluefin tuna, but we haven't confirmed that with the genetic testing yet," he said.

"But it looks highly likely they are because they've got some anatomical features which sort of set them apart from our regular southern bluefin tuna.

"They're very rare [in Australia]."

Fishers have travelled from across Australia to be part of the action. (Supplied: Victorian Fisheries Authority (VFA))

Researchers are collecting genetic samples and otoliths, or ear stones, including fish ear bones that can help determine their age, with recreational fishers and charter operators contributing to the research.

Discovery remains a mystery

Dr Hunt said why the tuna had appeared in such numbers off Lakes Entrance's coast remained a mystery.

He said the region's marine environment still held plenty of surprises.

"The eyes of the fishing community right now are on Lakes Entrance because it's just been amazing," he said.

"And it certainly sparks my sense of adventure to get down there and get on the water."

title: Desalination plant delayed, despite fears Eyre Peninsula could run out of water
text:
Work on a desalination plant in regional South Australia has been delayed by six months, past when the region was due to run out of clean drinking water.

SA Water has announced construction on the Eyre Peninsula Desalination Plant will be pushed back six months, to mid-2027, due to harder-than-usual granite affecting its underground boring

Consumer access to water will be "unchanged".

Residents of Port Lincoln and its surrounding areas were told they could run out of clean drinking water by 2026.

The 35,000 residents of the Eyre Peninsula draw drinking water from the Uley South Basin, which has been depleting at a rate described as "dire" by the state government.

The state government funded the then-$330 million Eyre Peninsula Desalination Plant project, which is now expected to cost approximately $470 million, at the Billy Lights Point coastal reserve.

Early works began in February 2025 and it was projected to deliver fresh water by the end of this year.

"We're a bit behind where we'd like to be," SA Water sustainable infrastructure general manager Peter Seltsikas said.

Peter Seltsikas says tunnelling delays have pushed out the plant's completion date. (ABC News: Brant Cumming)

"The pipelines are done, the desalination plant is substantially complete.

"But the tunnelling delay means the first water day is pushing out to the middle of next year."

Mr Seltsikas said higher-than-usual rains this year across the Eyre Peninsula had increased the water levels of the Uley South Basin.

"We have enough water this year to continue to supply our customers and when the desalination plant comes next year they'll continue to have secure water."

Cost blowouts and security concerns

Glen Ingham was the spokesperson for community action group Hands Off Boston Bay, which was opposed to the location of the desalination plant.

He said the delays were testing the government's claims the site is the "cheapest and quickest" option.

Glen Ingham was the spokesperson for Hands Off Boston Bay. (ABC Eyre Peninsula: Jodie Hamilton)

"Here we are now at the end of 2026 and they're [pushing the end date] to the middle of next year.

"I'm certain it will be beyond that and the cost blowout will be huge," he said.

In a statement, the state government said the revised budget of the project would be detailed once "contractual processes with delivery partners are complete".

Mr Seltsikas said the authority recognised the ongoing need to reduce water being taken from the basin.

"So we are very much concerned about water security," he said.

The state government said a revised Water Allocation Plan for the Southern Basins meant SA Water could extract water from the Uley South Basin and River Murray to meet consumer demand.

SA Water's groundwater allocation will reduce to 3.5 gigalitres per year in 2027-28, as the plant comes online.

A spokesperson said "it is not expected that water restrictions will be needed".

title: First openly gay male NBL player Isaac Humphries announces retirement
text:
Australia's first openly gay NBL player Isaac Humphries has announced he will retire from competitive basketball after struggling with an ongoing knee issue.

The 28-year-old centre has made a significant impact on and off the court, making history in 2022 when he came out as gay while playing for Melbourne United.

The Adelaide 36ers club champion made the announcement in a post on Instagram, saying he was "so sad to say goodbye like this".

"Sometimes life deals you cards that tell your story for you, and due to my continued knee injury I've had to make the incredibly difficult decision to retire," he said.

"I'll miss my teammates, the laughs, the trenches. I'll miss the fans, the noise and the feelings of having an entire community behind you."

Loading Instagram content

The former Boomer said he had given so much of his life to the sport, and it gave him a life he could never have imagined back.

"There is so much more to say, but for now, just thank you," he said.

"I hope the identity I created lives on in every person who wears my jersey, and in every place I was lucky enough to call home."

Humphries paid tribute to his contribution to both the club and Australian basketball, executive chairman Grant Kelley saying he has long admired Isaac's personal and professional courage.

"Beyond his impact on the court, Isaac has used his platform to advocate strongly for LGBTQI+ rights and mental health awareness, making a meaningful difference in the wider community," he said.

After a strong showing in Adelaide's NBL26 campaign, Humphries has not made an appearance for Adelaide in the current season due to his ongoing knee issue.

Humphries has played 173 games in the NBL and had a stint overseas in the NBA. (ABC News: Brant Cumming)

Humphries has played 173 games in the league, with 124 games at the Adelaide 36ers over five seasons.

He was named the club's MVP in the NBL24 season, returning to the club after a period with the Atlanta Hawks in the NBA and a one season stint at Melbourne United.

The Adelaide 36ers said Humphries will be continuing to work with the club, having accepted a non-playing role working in the community, marketing and commercial teams.

That’s the start of a Helen question. Polite, but extremely effective and probing. Her gentle demeanour belies her enormous contribution, particularly on government accountability and transparency. The people of Indi could not ask for a more diligent, serious and compassionate representative in public life. Related Article Haines attack Independent MP Helen Haines in critical condition after ‘attack’ outside her office Helen is warm and courageous. She will tell you to your face when she doesn’t agree with you, give you good, thought-through reasons, and then follow her conscience. She is funny. She is practical: she laughingly told me that as a bush midwife, she can make a splint out of an old newspaper. When I think of her like this, I am despairing. While Australia does not have a history of political violence, we do have the same trends as other democracies: rising aggression, threats and disruption. Reports of threats and harassment against federal parliamentarians to the Australian Federal Police rose from 279 in 2020-21 to more than 1000 in 2023-24. If you are in parliament, you feel it. You see the threats, the aggression particularly online. You try to ignore them.

Advertisement

What shocks me the most is that almost one in 10 Australians told last year’s McKinnon Index that violence can be justified for a political cause. We are successful as a country because we manage our disagreements through the ballot box, the parliament, the courts, through our institutions. But one in 10 seriously think violence is a political tool. As you look at the statistics, and particularly at online abuse, there is a deeply serious question – how did we get to a place where such aggression is socially permitted? And how do we turn it back? Allegra Spender (left) and Helen Haines (right) at Parliament House in Canberra in August. Dominic Lorrimer None of us have the answer, and we need to be careful about generalising from this specific incident which we still do not understand. But the broader trend of aggression towards politicians needs confronting. Many will point to the security services and their role in keeping politicians safe. That is critical and we need a serious reassessment. But just layering on the security of politicians delivers the opposite of the politics that Helen championed – engaged, available, local – and we mustn’t lose it. Security matters, but our culture I believe matters more and is harder to address.

Advertisement

Social media companies obviously have a role to play. Algorithms amplify outrage because outrage keeps us scrolling, and bots manipulate opinion at scale. ASIO has been clear that online radicalisation is a security risk – from violent Islamist extremism to violent misogyny. Regulation can help, but much of what the social media companies amplify is aggressive content that fellow Australians are putting out there. Editor's pick Haines attack Turn down the temperature: Spy chief’s urgent warning as Helen Haines remains in critical condition When abuse is normalised at the highest level, it makes room not only for extremism but for obsession and derangement. We don’t yet know the perpetrator’s motive or mental state, but Australian and international research shows many people who stalk, threaten or approach politicians live with serious, often untreated, mental illness. Though public discourse rarely makes such a person violent, it can shape who they fixate on and the story they tell themselves about why. It’s not just politicians who are abused and in danger – it’s teachers, nurses, supermarket workers. It’s the sort of abuse our grandmothers would have condemned. Somehow, all of us need to step up and say enough – we treat each other with respect, with dignity. We owe it to each other, whatever we agree or disagree on. No one in public life should ever expect violence. It is most shocking when it is directed at someone who never uses aggression as a political tool.

title: How tech geniuses became Hollywood’s favourite monster
text:
Lions and tigers and tech bros, oh my: Hollywood has a new go-to movie monster in 2026.

From The Social Reckoning to Artificial, today’s on-screen tech bros are more sinister than ever.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

A steely-eyed creature sits in its lair, dark clouds looming in the distance. Several prisoners tentatively enter, gathering the courage to deliver their meagre offerings to the unflinching force before them. The offering doesn’t suffice. With one severe glance, the creature has the prisoners fleeing, desperately hoping they need not return. This sounds like a scene from a horror film – the introduction of Hollywood’s newest flesh-eating beast. But this isn’t your average monster. It’s Mark Zuckerberg, Facebook’s co-founder and Meta chief executive. In Aaron Sorkin’s The Social Reckoning, the tech billionaire is the evil that lurks, the monster under the bed. But instead of a lair, he’s in a sterile office, emotionlessly watching overworked employees present dissatisfying statistics. From The Social Reckoning to Artificial, today’s tech bros appear more monstrous than ever. The film, a follow-up to 2010’s The Social Network (also penned by Sorkin), asks us to reconsider the definition of “monster”, suggesting it’s not fanged creatures and slasher killers we should be afraid of, but rather tech bro billionaires and their unbridled, unchecked power. Set around the 2021 Facebook Files leak, Zuckerberg is no longer the arrogant tech nerd portrayed by Jesse Eisenberg in The Social Network. Now, played by Jeremy Strong (Succession), he’s a robotic, dictatorial techpreneur, intent on increasing Facebook’s engagement even if it means intensifying hate speech, spreading misinformation and damaging mental health. The suggestion of safeguards, which could drop engagement by just one per cent, offends him. When urged to fact-check political ads on the social platform, he refuses, adamant that tech companies shouldn’t operate as arbiters of truth. Facebook, to him, is a corkboard – he can’t control what people pin to it. Jeremy Strong’s Mark Zuckerberg is more “evil lizard man” than arrogant anti-hero. Sony Pictures via AP

Advertisement

Sorkin insists his Zuckerberg is an “anti-hero” rather than a villain, a person with good intentions but poor carry-through. However, Strong’s unfeeling lizard-like performance suggests otherwise. The Social Reckoning is the first of several new movies to turn tech bros monstrous. Andrew Garfield will portray Sam Altman, co-founder of OpenAI, in Luca Guadagnino’s Artificial, landing January 21. Tracking the early development of artificial intelligence, the film’s trailer reads like a psychological horror, as Garfield’s Altman descends into a grim basement filled with guns. “We open Pandora’s Box together, the future is inevitable,” Garfield’s Altman says of AI in the trailer. “Countries will fall, industries are going to collapse, and we get to be the ones to shepherd people into this new world.” Loading It’s difficult to watch without shuddering, knowing that AI has been used to hack into government systems and to mislead using deepfakes and chatbot hallucinations. A former employee from AI safety and research firm Anthropic even warned that AI companies are “gambling with our lives”. Garfield has acknowledged the insidiousness, telling Variety he no longer uses ChatGPT. “I got a bit scared … I felt a little mistrusting of the technology. It feels like the people who are encouraging us to use the technologies don’t exactly know its capacities themselves. That feels a little irresponsible”. Andrew Garfield as Sam Altman and Yura Borisov as Ilya Sutskever in Artificial. Yannis Drakoulidis

Advertisement

Fellow OpenAI co-founder Elon Musk has also attracted Hollywood’s attention. Alex Gibney’s Musk, a nearly four-hour documentary yet to set an Australian release, traces the tech billionaire’s stint in government and ownership of SpaceX, Tesla and X. Musk’s power is so immense that he’s described in the documentary’s teaser trailer as the “Earth’s most unchecked man” and, more concerningly, a “nuke”. Boasting a net worth of nearly $US1 trillion, Musk is the world’s richest person, and with such wealth comes great power. Musk’s lawyers threatened to file a defamation suit ahead of the film’s release, though no suit has officially been filed. Loading Artificial, meanwhile, was dropped by Amazon in June shortly after the company signed a lucrative deal with OpenAI. Coincidence? Luckily, Neon picked it up. Similarly, Sony reportedly received a “strongly worded letter” from Meta after it caught wind of The Social Reckoning. Though these films will land on screens, they’ve had to fight to get there. Perhaps the most anticipated “tech monster” to hit cinemas is Elizabeth Holmes. The disgraced Theranos founder, who’s currently in prison, will be the focus of You Can See Everything, a documentary by Nathan Fielder (The Rehearsal) and Lance Oppenheim (Some Kind of Heaven) landing on November 12. Though only acquitted for defrauding investors, Holmes’ work on the failed blood-testing startup – which provided inaccurate and unreliable blood tests – could have eventually cost lives. Yet in the documentary’s trailer, Holmes insists she did nothing wrong and has “nothing to hide” whilst staring, unblinking, at Fielder, as if trying to consume him with her eyes alone. It’s arguably scarier than any horror film as this is a real person, who has done terrible things for the sake of money and success, and who still fails to acknowledge their ethical shortcomings. Elizabeth Holmes’ stare is beyond unsettling in the trailer for You Can See Everything. YouTube

Advertisement

This is where today’s tech monsters differ from tech bros of the past. Eisenberg’s Mountainhead (2025), a film about four fictional tech tycoons isolating from an economic disaster in a secluded cabin, makes light of their buffoonish behaviour and ineptitude. Jemaine Clement’s tech mogul antagonist in M3GAN 2.0 (2025) is a mash-up of Silicon Valley figures, thus explaining his larger-than-life performance that can hardly be taken seriously. Australian director Leigh Whannell’s The Invisible Man was arguably ahead of the curve in 2020, featuring an exaggeratedly evil tech boss who fakes his suicide and uses a camouflage suit to stalk his ex-partner. Meanwhile, earlier films with real-life tech tycoons, such as The Social Network and Steve Jobs, depicted them more generously. Zuckerberg was a misguided nerd; Jobs was an obsessive genius. Even the fictionalised series about Holmes, The Dropout, showed her dancing to Lil Wayne at one point. They were flawed, but certainly didn’t appear to have the capacity to end the world. Jesse Eisenberg’s Mark Zuckerberg was more twerpy than evil. Sony It seems we can no longer hide behind such levity and fiction. From The Social Reckoning to Artificial, today’s tech bro films are beyond bleak. They capture periods that felt like rock bottom, such as when extremists (many of whom were radicalised on Facebook) stormed the US Capitol. Yet, things have only gotten worse. While earlier films warned of what may come, these films scream: “It’s too late”. That’s scarier than any masked killer or bloodthirsty beast. The Social Reckoning is in cinemas now. I was working with a private client who had a lump-sum of money available to invest. We’d spent some time getting her clarity on her financial position, adding some structure to her finances, and building her understanding of investing. This gave her some assurance, calmed her nerves and improved her confidence in preparation for investing. But the money was still sitting there, in her account – uninvested. Despite all the progress, she felt restless: that task was looming over her head, waiting to be ticked off the checklist. The sky isn’t falling – you can take your time to invest sensibly and strategically. Simon Letch This is something I see in clients a lot: urgency, restlessness, impatience. This feeling of: “I should be further ahead than where I am right now,” or “I’m behind”, or “This is taking too long.” That’s understandable. There is messaging everywhere that reinforces this: from gloom-and-doom headlines that make you lose sleep at night, to the never-ending comparison one can fall into on social media, so no matter how far you get, it never feels like it’s enough.

Advertisement

Many people are convinced this anxiety is helpful. It’s what motivates you to get things done, to achieve and progress. To some extent, that may be true. Editor's pick Opinion

Ask an expert Rich, successful ... now what? How to reignite your financial drive Paridhi Jain Money contributor However, often, this anxiety also pushes people into rushed decisions that just cause more anxiety down the track. For example, you have a lump sum of money you know you “should” invest, but you don’t know how – so you hand it over to the first financial adviser you talk to or buy the first property some family member says to because you just want it off your plate. For a short time, you’re relieved. But quickly, you’re now worried about whether it was the right move. One of the most powerful but underrated skills you can develop on your wealth journey is the ability to tolerate anxiety without reacting to it. Here are some perspective shifts that will help:

Advertisement

Learn to measure progress differently When it comes to money, we are often so anxious to fast-forward to the outcome that we don’t consider anything else progress. We want more money in the bank, we want the house bought, the money invested, the ROI delivered – we want tangible results, and we want them fast. But that’s not how it works. There could be many steps before you arrive at the outcome. Maybe you never had much exposure to the idea of investing until later in your life. Perhaps it took a while for you to overcome your fear of risk. Getting to the finish line isn’t progress – every step towards the finish line is. Maybe you never thought it was even possible for someone without a professional financial background to invest on their own. Maybe you first had to figure out how to stay out of debt and save consistently before investing was an option. Maybe you had to make a few mistakes and lose a bit of money to learn a few lessons.

Advertisement

If you’re impatiently waiting until you finally have $X in investments or $Y net-worth you’re missing (and devaluing) all the progress you’ve made until that point. Getting to the finish line isn’t progress – every step towards the finish line is. Sustainable progress beats fast wins Everyone will sell you fast results – because fast sells. But having now supported hundreds of clients in creating (collectively) millions of dollars of financial outcomes – I can tell you that it’s usually the ones who aren’t trying to rush to the end, who end up growing the fastest long-term. The ones who have achievable goals that they can be excited about. The ones who aren’t measuring progress solely by the number, but by how much they’re learning and growing. The ones who are enjoying the added clarity and confidence that comes with figuring out one more piece of the puzzle – knowing, trusting, that piece by piece, the puzzle will be completed. This is what gives them the ability to stay the course, without getting tired, frustrated, impatient, burnt-out – and ultimately, why they get faster, bigger results, long term.

Advertisement

This takes the ability to enjoy the journey – and not just the outcome. This can be tough when it comes to wealth because – well, of course you just want the outcome, duh. Everyone just wants the money, right? Surely, no one enjoys something as dry and boring as investing, right? Editor's pick Opinion

Collectables Not just nostalgia: Your old toy cars could be a secret goldmine Stephen Crafti Money contributor Listen, I get it. I disliked finance so much in university, I switched my major to economics. But I didn’t have to find enjoyment in the subject itself – I found satisfaction in building my financial confidence, in figuring out something that previously seemed too complex and so on. So, celebrate every milestone; see each step as “one-step-forward” instead of “look-how-far-I-still-have-to-go”; and find satisfaction in your own growth, not just the pot of gold at the end. title: Cirque du Soleil is exuberant old-fashioned circus pleasure, plus other new shows this week
text:
Moore Park Entertainment Quarter, October 18, until January 3.

Roll up – the world’s biggest circus, Cirque du Soleil, is back in town with KOOZA. A throwback to a more interactive, traditional style of circus, KOOZA was created in 2007 by director David Shiner as a departure from the huge theatrical spectacles that had, by then, almost defined Cirque du Soleil’s immensely popular style. Under Shiner’s vision, Stéphane Roy’s set evokes an old-fashioned carnival, and Marie-Chantale Vaillancourt’s costumes are a rainbow of acrobat stripes in nostalgic circus colours.

KOOZA by Cirque du Soleil offers a buffet of spectacular circus skills including contortionists, aerial silks and a devastatingly romantic unicycle duet. Matt Beard & Bernard Letendre

Shiner – a trained clown himself – sent in the clowns. The moment you enter the spiral-patterned big top theatre, it’s hard to spill popcorn without hitting one. Pacing through the audience, the clowns initially favour banter over slapstick, giving the impression that the cast of a North American comedy club has run away with the circus. Once the show begins though, the clowns pull out all the stops with mime, slapstick, and physical theatre.

Kooza features jaw-dropping displays of acrobatic prowess. Matt Beard & Bernard Letendre

While clowns in other Cirque du Soleil shows might have a touch more European arthouse whimsy, these clowns bear the stamp of Shiner’s modern American comedy and vaudeville interests. Their ringleader, Mark Gindick’s slouching, wise-cracking mad King, chants “CHUG, CHUG, CHUG!” as soon as he spies the cans of drink in my and my guest’s hands. He’s accompanied by a bumbling henchman duo (Miguel Berlanga Madroño and Duncan Cameron) straight from a children’s action comedy film. There’s even a fluffy clown-dog who urinates real water.

The Day of the Dead-inspired “Skeleton Dance” has a chorus of skeleton showgirls – just some of the show’s vibrant sets and costumes. Matt Beard & Bernard Letendre

For those requiring a dose of schmaltz, the clowning frames the central narrative: a story about a child-like elfin character known as the Innocent, who arrives complete with kite and upturned red nose just in case you missed the fact he’s meant to represent your inner child.

Performed with great sympathy by Alexandr Yudintsev, the Innocent encounters Mitch Wynter’s dapper Trickster, who prompts him to explore the wider world.

One of the many characters in KOOZA. Matt Beard & Bernard Letendre

Enter the abundant buffet of circus acts the wide-eyed Innocent encounters along the way. There are contortionists, aerial silks, a devastatingly romantic unicycle duet (Anastasiia Shkandybina and Dmytro Dudnyk), an outstandingly charismatic diabolo act (Wei-Liang Lin), a wheel of death scene channelling WWE, and nail-biting highwires and a teeterboard.

All are of Cirque du Soleil’s usual high standard: tightly choreographed, impeccably performed, and eliciting a constant audience rollercoaster of gasps and cheers.

It’s all accompanied by a live band belting out Jean-François Côté’s original music from the top floor of the carnival set. The music and its visual presentation are broad for Cirque du Soleil: following Shiner’s eclectic palette, it spans from the usual ethereal ambient to musical theatre, Bollywood, burlesque, vaudeville, and cabaret. The Day of the Dead-inspired “Skeleton Dance”, featuring Jessica Fox as the Soul Singer, even has a chorus of skeleton showgirls, ostrich feathers bouncing with every strut.

Other commentators have found the clowning excessive, so whether you enjoy KOOZA may come down to personal tastes in comedy style. But with world-class acrobatics and Cirque du Soleil’s extraordinary production values, KOOZA makes an exuberant case for the pleasure of old-fashioned circus.

Chantal Nguyen reviewed a preview performance of KOOZA.

Critical Resources has muscled its way deeper into South America, securing exclusivity over a third gold project in Suriname, just a nine-iron from a monster mine. The company’s new Gadu Manda project sits a mere four kilometres west of Chinese giant Zijin Mining’s Rosebel open pit gold mine, which has churned out more than six million ounces of gold since 2004. The savvy deal boosts the company’s significant ground package in the gold-rich nation to 228 square kilometres, including the new 29-square-kilometre Gadu Manda project, the recently acquired 164-square-kilometre Gonini and its 35-square-kilometre Greenstars gold project. Notably, the company secured exclusive rights over all three on staged low-risk terms in less than a month. Third-party small-scale open pit artisanal workings at Critical Resources’ Gadu Manda project in Suriname, 4km from the giant 6-million-ounce Rosebel gold mine. Under the terms of the latest deal, Critical has entered an exclusivity agreement to acquire a 90 per cent interest in Gadu Manda for a staggered consideration of US$200,000 (A$287,000) in cash over two years and 2.5 million Critical Resources shares, along with a A$287,000 minimum exploration commitment. The arrangement includes a US$10,000 (A$14,326) exclusivity fee, giving the company 60 days to conduct its due diligence. With management already having boots on the ground in Suriname, the company is well placed to fast-track due diligence at Gadu Manda alongside its other recently secured gold projects. Suriname has quietly become a hotspot for global gold capital over the past few years. Precious metal production generated US$2 billion (A$2.87B) in earnings for the nation in 2024 and accounted for almost 80 per cent of its total exports.

Advertisement

‘The project is located about 4km from the pits of Zijin’s Rosebel gold mine, on ground already being worked by small-scale miners.’ Critical Resources managing director Tim Wither That kind of output has not gone unnoticed. The region has seen a flurry of corporate activity of late, led by Zijin’s US$360 million (A$516M) acquisition of the Rosebel mine in 2023. More recently, gold giant Gold Fields tipped C$77 million (A$78.28M) into explorer Founders Metals for a 19.9 per cent stake. At the same time, private investment house La Mancha has taken significant positions in other Canadian-listed explorers active in Suriname. The real sizzle in this deal is the project’s address. Big gold deposits rarely live in isolation. Gadu Manda’s proximity to the Rosebel mine, which boasts a whopping 11.6 million ounces of gold, is the kind of nearology that gets geologists leaping out of bed in the morning. Adding to the intrigue, small-scale artisanal miners have already been working the northern part of the Gadu Manda permit area, with pits and trenches exposing quartz veining. This potentially gives Critical a ready-made set of walk-up targets, with the old-timers having already done the initial sniffing for near-surface gold. All three of Critical’s new projects sit within the Guiana Shield, a well-endowed but relatively underexplored geological province, considered the South American counterpart to West Africa’s phenomenally rich Birimian Shield. While the Birimian belts host more than 500 million ounces of discovered gold, the Guiana Shield lays claim to a still-impressive 100-million-ounce inventory, suggesting there may be plenty of room for new discoveries.

Advertisement

Critical Resources managing director Tim Wither said: “Gadu Manda will be a strong addition to our Suriname portfolio. The Project is located about 4 km from the pits of Zijin’s Rosebel mine, on ground already being worked by small-scale miners. This gives us a head start in developing our understanding of the Project. Together with Gonini and Greenstars, Gadu Manda will give Critical Resources three granted gold projects in a proven gold province. We are currently in Suriname completing due diligence on all three projects, including site visits, while high-level structural targeting work is under way.” The company’s other recently acquired Suriname projects include Gonini,which lies in the historic Sara Creek district within the Marowijne greenstone belt, just 66km from Newmont’s multi-million-ounce Merian gold mine. While gold has been mined in the district for 150 years, the company says there is no record of modern systematic exploration at Gonini. Its second asset, the Greenstars project, sits just 35km west of Zijin’s Rosebel mine. It has road access from the capital, Paramaribo and contains active small-scale alluvial workings, confirming the presence of gold in the local system. Critical says structural targeting by Guiana Shield geophysics specialists GexplOre is now underway across the permits as well as 6000 square kilometres of the surrounding greenstone belt. While the company is clearly making an aggressive push into South American gold, it also holds several other cards in its hand, including the flagship Mavis Lake lithium project in Ontario, Canada, which already holds an 8-million-tonne resource grading 1.07 per cent lithium oxide.

Advertisement

In addition, Critical owns the Halls Peak base metals project in New South Wales, with an inferred resource of 840,000 tonnes at 3.7 per cent zinc and 1.5 per cent lead, and is evaluating next-generation solid-state lithium-ion battery intellectual property in the United States. The company also has interests in a suite of gold, antimony and tungsten prospects in New Zealand, giving it exposure across multiple critical commodities and jurisdictions. For now, however, all eyes are on Suriname. With management on site and a clear strategy to build a significant landholding next door to a world-class mine, Critical appears to have its foot on the accelerator. The company is betting that where there’s smoke, there’s fire – and being just 4km from a 6-million-ounce bonfire seems potentially a very good place to start looking. October 20, 2026 — 2:03pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Many car enthusiasts fondly recall memories of their Holdens and Fords from the 1960s and ’70s. While few held on to these prized automobiles, considerably more still have the model car taking pride-of-place on their shelves, recalling a time when drivers such Peter Brock and Allan Moffat took out titles on the racetrack at Bathurst. These miniature toys, often diecast, still hold memories as well as their value – many toy cars are priced in the hundreds and, occasionally, in the thousands of dollars. A selection of valuable model cars, including a toy Batman car from the ’60s. Jamie Brown, Car Models of Braidwood, Back to Cool For Daniel Parsons, who owns Car Models of Braidwood, a historic township in the Southern Tablelands of NSW, it’s the adults rather than children coming into the store or buying online. “The Holden VF Commodore toy cars are popular. Take the Ford Focus RS WRC08 for $230 or the Chevrolet Camaro for the same amount. It’s a healthy sum given the Chevrolet is a re-release of a 1968 model,” says Parsons.

Advertisement

Some prices of these toy cars can also be attributed to models, such as the Holden and Ford, that are no longer manufactured in Australia. “The saying ‘once they’re gone, they’re gone’ applies to the toys as much as the real thing,” adds Parsons, who sees the choice of toy car as often responding to either the owner’s present car or something they experienced driving as a young adult. Editor's pick Opinion

Collectables Some designer clothing attracts a collector’s premium. But which? Stephen Crafti Money contributor The word “vintage” in the toy world is often used to describe toys only a few decades old. Take a Holden VK Commodore Group C. The winner of the Bathurst 1000 in 1984, driven by Brock, can even be more valuable if the owner has the entire series (each car driven at Bathurst came with a set with numbers emblazoned on the hood and car doors since Bathurst started in 1938) – upwards of $10,000. Peter Neagle, who owns Paul’s Toys in Niddrie, Melbourne, has been surrounded by vintage car toys since his late father, Jack, opened the store in 1953. There are Matchbox cars, Dinky vintage diecast cars as well as Corgi, many from the 1960s through to the ’80s. Critica Limited has kicked the door down with a blockbuster scoping study for its wholly owned Jupiter rare earths project in Western Australia, outlining a potential world-class development sporting a whopping pre-tax net present value (NPV) of $2.67 billion. Using an eight per cent discount rate, the study forecasts a pre-tax internal rate of return (IRR) of 56 per cent. Pre-production capital is estimated at A$555.5 million, with total life-of-mine capital of A$606.2 million, including sustaining and closure costs. Payback is estimated at two years after operations begin. Critica’s Jupiter project in Western Australia’s Mid-West region, 270km from Geraldton. The 14-year operation is projected to generate $12.3 billion in sales revenue and $5.64 billion in pre-tax free cash flow, delivering a hefty average annual return before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation (EBITDA) of A$446 million. The assessment mapped out an eight-million-tonne-a-year conventional open-pit operation, targeting 107.3 million tonnes of ore grading 1879 parts per million (ppm) total rare earth oxides (TREO) over the mine’s life. Indicated mineral resources account for 97 per cent, or 104 million tonnes of the material. Inferred resources account for the remaining 3 per cent.

Advertisement

‘The Jupiter Scoping Study delivers a pre-tax NPV₈ of A$2.7 billion and provides a clear technical foundation for the next phase of development at Jupiter.’ Critica Limited chief executive officer Jacob Deysel Planned output represents just six per cent of Jupiter’s mammoth 1.7-billion-tonne resource, grading 1700ppm TREO, including an initial 160-million-tonne indicated resource. Critica says the remaining 94 per cent lies outside the mine plan, leaving scope for resource conversion and mine-life extensions, subject to further work. Annual production of contained rare earth oxides in mixed rare earth carbonate (MREC) is estimated at 8,300 tonnes, based on an overall recovery of 58 per cent, a grade similar to that achieved in earlier metallurgical testwork. The MREC basket includes neodymium, praseodymium, dysprosium, terbium and yttrium. Using a “beneficiation-first” approach, the processing flowsheet combines magnetic separation and flotation to concentrate the rare earths before sending the upgraded material through the more expensive chemical treatment process, known as hydrometallurgy. Testwork achieved a 14-fold TREO upgrade while rejecting up to 95 per cent of feed mass, massively reducing downstream plant requirements and costs. Critica Limited chief executive officer Jacob Deysel said: “The Jupiter Scoping Study is a major milestone for Critica, demonstrating the potential for a large-scale rare earths development with compelling preliminary economics and a production target overwhelmingly underpinned by Indicated Mineral Resources.”

Advertisement

The model’s base case assumes a gross MREC basket value of US$52.80 (A$81) per kilogram and 75 per cent payability, using an exchange-rate assumption of 65 cents. Adding another layer of financial appeal to Jupiter’s already impressive numbers, Critica’s economic modelling has factored in the Australian Government’s Critical Minerals Production Tax Incentive (CMPTI), a refundable offset of 10 per cent of eligible Australian processing expenditure for up to 10 years. The incentive could deliver up to $264.1 million in benefits, subject to eligibility and qualifying expenditure. Iron, gallium and scandium have no base-case value, leaving them as potential upside. The MREC basket includes neodymium, praseodymium, dysprosium, terbium and yttrium. With the financial foundations now mapped out, Critica has turned its attention to the next development hurdles, pencilling in a prefeasibility study (PFS) from early 2027 to mid-2028, followed by a definitive feasibility study (DFS) through to the end of 2029. Work will include drilling and resource conversion, process optimisation and integrated pilot-plant testing, environmental and heritage studies, product qualification, offtake and partnership discussions, and funding. The development blueprint envisaged construction kicking off in 2030 with first MREC production and sales in 2032. No official reserve has been declared as yet, with Critica keen to emphasise the preliminary study does not guarantee the production target or economic outcomes. The timing of the study is fortuitous, landing as governments seek to diversify rare earth supply chains beyond China. The International Energy Agency says demand for magnet rare earths has doubled since 2015 and is expected to rise by more than 30 per cent by 2030. Australia’s Critical Minerals Strategic Reserve includes rare earths, adding to a more favourable policy backdrop for domestic development.

Critica describes Jupiter as Australia’s largest clay-hosted rare earth resource. It sits 70km south-west of Mount Magnet and 270km east of Geraldton, near road, gas and power infrastructure. Jupiter is one of six rare earth discoveries in Critica’s wholly owned Brothers project, positioning the company to potentially unlock a much bigger district-scale rare earths play. With such robust initial numbers based on just a fraction of Jupiter’s vast resource, Critica has laid out a clear pathway to advance what could become a significant new source of magnet rare earths for Western supply chains. title: Pregnancy discrimination remains widespread in Australian workplaces
text:
IN BRIEF Nearly half of mothers report discrimination during pregnancy, parental leave or returning to work.

An Australian Human Rights Commission report found pregnancy discrimination hasn't decreased over the last decade.

After being passed up for an associate principal role at a school, a woman went on maternity leave to have her first baby.

When she returned to work, she expected to go back to her role in leadership.

Instead, her principal told her she would come back as a music teacher.

"He just said, the school no longer needed my role," the Perth woman told AAP.

"I don't have any formal music qualifications ... He gave me the job he considered to be the least important."

The mother-of-two, who spoke on the condition of anonymity as she still works in the state school system, considered taking action against her principal.

She spoke to the Fair Work Ombudsman and her union, but decided not to pursue a claim.

"My life was already so full, I didn't want to take more time away from being with my kid," she said.

"And it would just be rough to work for someone that you had legally fought with to have that job."

READ MORE Gabriela was playing at the top of her sport. Then she fell pregnant

In another case, Alana, from Melbourne, worked at a hydrotherapy service for babies and tried to take time off to be with her one-year-old when he was hospitalised.

"I gave a few days' notice, and she [the manager] got really, really angry and lost it, and said it's unacceptable, if your son is sick, you have to call your mother or a babysitter," she said.

"Another time he was sick ... she said that I had to have my husband take him, or I wouldn't have a job."

Almost half of mothers, 49 per cent, experienced discrimination during pregnancy, parental leave or return to work, a 2014 Australian Human Rights Commission (AHRC) study found.

Sex Discrimination Commissioner Anna Cody says pregnancy discrimination and discrimination on the basis of carers' responsibility remains widespread. Source: Getty / Thomas Trutschel/Photothek via Getty Images

About 91 per cent did not lodge formal complaints out of stress, fear of retaliation or lack of legal awareness.

Little has changed, with pregnancy, breastfeeding and family responsibility discrimination remaining "a significant and widespread workplace issue" in 2026, an AHRC report released on Tuesday found.

The number of alleged pregnancy discrimination complaints the AHRC received rose from 54 in 2021 to 72 in 2025.

The AHRC met with 84 stakeholders, including industry, community, advocates, lawyers, unions and academics.

READ MORE Pregnant women face widespread workplace discrimination, report finds

Recurring patterns of discrimination were identified, including "sham" redundancies and job loss during pregnancy or parental leave, diminished duties when returning to work, and refusal of flexible work arrangements.

Harms were amplified for First Nations, migrant, racially-marginalised, disabled, and LGBTQI+ communities, who experienced intersecting forms of discrimination.

"It was really clear that pregnancy discrimination, and discrimination on the basis of carers' responsibility, is widespread and hasn't changed significantly in the last 12 years," Sex Discrimination Commissioner Anna Cody said.

She said employers needed to change how they conceptualise work, with flexible working arrangements made a presumption unless an employer rebuts, and the 12-month service requirement to access unpaid parental leave eliminated.

The AHRC made 18 recommendations, including amending the Sex Discrimination Act to ban indirect discrimination based on family responsibilities, and limiting redundancies during or immediately after parental leave.

title: A pandemic-era record has returned. The next chapter looks different
text:
In brief Australians are moving from the nation's cities to its regions at an increasing rate.

Data shows some are looking further afield than traditional satellite cities.

Australians are moving from the cities to the regions at rates not seen since the COVID-19 pandemic, with a regional Western Australian city the fastest-growing hotspot.

The Commonwealth Bank and the Regional Australia Institute's (RAI) latest Regional Movers Index shows capital-to-regional migration in the June quarter had matched the record levels of the same quarter in 2021.

The report reveals capital city residents moving to the regions outnumber those moving in the opposite direction by 30 per cent.

While established satellite cities such as the Sunshine Coast and Geelong continue to attract the largest share of movers, the data shows some are looking further afield.

The Western Australian regional centre of Greater Geraldton had the highest year-on-year growth, with net inflows from capitals rising by 225 per cent to June 2026.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

NSW's Clarence Valley and South Australia's Murray Bridge ranked second and third, with growth of 167.3 per cent and 150 per cent, respectively.

Queensland's Toowoomba recorded growth of 147.1 per cent after topping the rankings in the March 2026 quarter. Bathurst in NSW rounded out the top five with growth of 122.4 per cent.

Sydney and Melbourne continue to be the largest sources of regional movers, respectively accounting for 52 per cent and 36 per cent of net outflows across all capital cities.

In overall numbers, the Sunshine Coast, about 100km north of Brisbane, remained the most popular regional destination, receiving 8.7 per cent of the share of total net migration.

It was followed by Greater Geelong, south of Melbourne, with 5 per cent, Lake Macquarie on the NSW Central Coast with 4.1 per cent, Fraser Coast in Queensland with 3.9 per cent and Moorabool in Victoria with 3.6 per cent.

The inter-regional migration index, tracking movement between regional areas, was above its long-term average but below its June quarter peak in 2023.

When including inter-regional migration, Central Goldfields in Victoria, about 140km northwest of Melbourne, experienced the strongest growth, with net internal migration inflows increasing 312 per cent over the year.

It was followed by Burdekin in north Queensland at 285 per cent, Snowy Monaro in southern NSW at 233 per cent, and the Tablelands and Douglas, both in far north Queensland, at 223 per cent and 221 per cent, respectively.

While Burdekin's growth was mostly driven by arrivals from capital cities, Tablelands benefited from a mix of capital city and regional migration.

Growth in the other regions was primarily driven by migration from other regional areas.

Country appeal remains 'incredibly strong'

RAI chief Liz Ritchie said 2026's high June quarter numbers were particularly noteworthy as internal migration typically slowed during this period, with fewer Australians tending to move during the cooler months.

"This tells us the appeal of country living remains incredibly strong all year round, even outside the traditional peak moving periods," she said.

"Australians are increasingly considering a broader range of regional communities when deciding where to live, with the benefits of regional living extending beyond popular coastal towns and inland communities."

Ritchie said the RAI's regional population planning report had found regional growth outpaced government projections by 114,000 people over the past decade.

"With more Australians choosing regional communities, we need population planning that anticipates growth and ensures housing, infrastructure and essential services keep pace," she said.

Commonwealth Bank's regional and agribusiness banking executive general manager, Kylie Allen, attributed North Queensland's growth to investment in diversifying local economies.

Burdekin, south of Townsville and home to Ayr and Home Hill, was supported by agriculture, manufacturing and renewable energy, she said.

The Tablelands, inland from Cairns and including Atherton, benefited from strong agribusiness and tourism sectors.

Douglas, which includes Port Douglas north of Cairns, was supported by a thriving tourism industry and ongoing investment in local infrastructure.

"Across northern Queensland, local investment is helping regions capitalise on their distinct strengths and drive broader economic growth," she said.

"When local businesses invest and expand, the benefits flow through the wider economy, creating jobs, attracting skilled workers and strengthening the services and supply chains that help regional communities thrive."

title: Millions risk fines as key tax deadline nears. Here's what to do
text:
Time is running out for millions of Australians yet to lodge their 2025-26 tax return.

The Australian Taxation Office (ATO) has already received 9 million income tax returns, but it says around 2 million people are yet to submit theirs ahead of the deadline, with late lodgers potentially facing fines.

When is the 2026 tax return deadline?

This year's deadline is Monday 2 November.

The last day of October is traditionally the due date for self-prepared tax returns, but when the 31st falls on a Saturday, the deadline moves to the next business day.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

If you are using a tax agent to file your return, the ATO says you must be on their books by 31 October.

ATO assistant commissioner Anita Challen warns taxpayers using this option should also ensure their tax profession is registered with the Tax Practitioners Board.

"Taxpayers should be sceptical of anyone making promises that sound too good to be true," she said.

"No reputable tax professional will encourage you to inflate your deductions, guarantee a refund amount, or claim they can fast-track ATO processing."

What happens if you lodge your tax return late?

If you fail to lodge your return before the due date, the ATO will first try to warn you over the phone or in writing before issuing a penalty.

For taxpayers struggling to file on time or experiencing extenuating circumstances, the ATO says to call and talk to an ATO officer who may be able to offer additional support, including extra time to lodge or pay.

If you are given a fine, you'll receive a notice in writing with the amount and the due date for payment. The payment will be due at least 14 days after the notice is given.

How much is the ATO late lodgement fine?

The fine is calculated based on one penalty unit for every 28 days (or part of that period) that the document is overdue. The maximum for an individual is five penalty units.

A penalty unit for a federal organisation like the ATO is currently valued at $364. So, an individual may be fined up to $1,820.

The range is multiplied for medium and larger entities.

title: Australia's growing cities face an unexpected challenge beneath the surface
text:
In brief Some metropolitan cemeteries are expected to run out of burial space by the early 2030s.

Cremation and alternative forms of deathcare are becoming increasingly common in Australia.

Australians are familiar with the housing crisis, but there's a lesser-known land battle occurring right beneath our feet.

Some metropolitan cemeteries are running out of space, and it's raising questions about the accessibility of burial practices and rise of alternative forms of deathcare.

Among them is Rookwood Cemetery in Sydney's west, which is the largest necropolis in the southern hemisphere.

It rivals the size of many suburbs, spanning more than 280 hectares, and has been operating for almost 160 years.

Rob Smart is the acting CEO of Metropolitan Memorial Parks, which manages eight Crown land cemeteries in NSW, including Rookwood.
