Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

He said the company maximises operating space and is trying to acquire more land but almost all of their cemeteries are expected to reach capacity by the early 2030s.

"As our larger sites do run out of land, that puts pressure on all of the other sites that might still have land," he told SBS News.

It's not just Metropolitan Memorial Parks, with many cemeteries in major cities predicting they will reach capacity within the decade.

That's in part due to the growth of urban areas, according to Ben Kelly, the CEO of the Australasian Cemeteries and Crematoria Association.

While cities have continued to grow, Ben Kelly said we haven't been building new cemeteries. Source: Supplied

"You look at Rookwood in Sydney, that was right on the outskirts, and now, that's almost an inner suburb," he said.

"It's just our cities have grown, we just haven't continued building cemeteries."

Another challenge, Kelly said, is that some residents don't want to live next them, while governments had other funding priorities.

"They're worried, they'll ... reduce house prices, that type of thing or they just find them spooky and they're not," he said.

The NSW government is considering converting Carnarvon Golf Club in the Sydney suburb of Lidcombe into a new cemetery, a proposal criticised by some community members, including Auburn MP Lynda Voltz.

READ MORE Kath hosted her late partner Nigel's wake while he was still alive

She addressed NSW parliament in May regarding risks of flooding in the area.

"At first glance, this proposal may be presented as a practical response to the growing demand for burial space but when you take a closer look, a different picture emerges," she said.

"The planning falls short, key risks are being brushed over and yet the environmental consequences are hard to ignore ... flooding here is frequent."

The proposal remains under review.

According to the Australian Bureau of Statistics, last year there were more than 188,000 registered deaths in the nation. Kelly says roughly 75 to 85 per cent of Australians are now cremated.

But some faith groups, including Islam and Judaism, do not permit the practice.

In 2023, the Vatican updated its guidance on cremation, allowing Catholics to request that a small portion of their relative's ashes be preserved in a "place of significance to them".

Smart believes all Australians should be given the option of a traditional burial.

"Australia is a multicultural country and while we do have a broad range of faiths and cultures within Australia, I think, we need to be able to provide choice," he said.

"To say to people, you can't follow your cultural, your faith-based requirements is very restrictive on the individuals, or the families or the communities."

DIY commemorations

While some cemeteries are running out of space for new burials, Hannah Gould, from the University of Melbourne's DeathTech Research Team, said there is often room to keep cremated remains.

She said the way Australians are approaching death and memorial celebrations is also gradually changing, such as with the rise of 'do it yourself' commemorations.

Hannah Gould says Australians are approaching death commemorations differently than in the past. Source: Supplied

"When it comes to the handling of the body, the vast majority of those processes need to be done by professionals," she said.

"It's not legal in this country to bury somebody or to cremate somebody yourself but kind of everything else now is is increasingly being done by family members and friends.

"You just organise to like get together at the pub with friends, as opposed to having a formal funeral ceremony that's run by a funeral director."

After cremation, ashes can be kept in a permanent place like a cemetery or scattered on private property or certain public areas with permission.

Ashes can also grow into a living memorial tree, be preserved in a memory rock, turned into jewellery, a diamond or even fireworks.

Alternative forms of disposition including sea burials, green or biodegradable burials and full-body human cryonics have taken place around the world.

Upright burials, where the deceased are buried standing, feet first, are also becoming more popular.

Another space-saving measure is renewable tenure, where burial plots are leased for set amounts of time — usually 25, 50 or 99 years — rather than in perpetuity.

If the grave is not renewed after a grace period, the plot can eventually be reused.

It's widely practised in South Australia, while in Western Australia, graves are sold with a 25-year lease known as a grant of right of burial.

Whether a person wants to be cremated or buried, Kelly believes it's important people have conversations about death and disposition while they're still living.

"Trying to plan after the fact of a loved one dying is so difficult," he said.

"So, if they can get in early and have that conversation, you know, put a note on the fridge, a post-it of 'I want to be cremated', it starts a conversation and gets people talking."

title: This tax hasn't changed in 26 years. Some say Australia can no longer afford that
text:
In brief Increasing the GST from 10 to 15 per cent would raise about $76 billion a year, according to the Grattan Institute.

Another recent study found that a GST increase might hurt lower-income households less than commonly thought.

The last time an Australian government owed this much debt, the country was still paying off a world war — except for the COVID-19 pandemic.

As government debt climbs, the Grattan Institute has proposed a controversial solution: hike one tax, cut another, and put more money in welfare recipients' pockets.

In a new report, the think tank argues that raising the country's Goods and Services Tax (GST) and using the money to cut income taxes and boost welfare payments is a solution to the debt issue.

GST is a flat 10 per cent tax applied to the price of most goods and services sold or consumed in Australia.

According to the report, titled Budget reboot: How to fund Australia's future, cost-of-living pressures, growing demand for social services, and higher borrowing costs are the drivers of the Australian government's mounting debt.

News that makes sense Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox. Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

It suggests the situation could worsen in the coming years, with factors such as an ageing population, climate change, and high interest rates forcing the government to spend more.

According to the report, raising GST from 10 per cent to 15 per cent and expanding it to include all food would create a more resilient budget.

Why raising GST has become a 'political no-go zone'

Since its introduction by former prime minister John Howard, which came into effect in July 2000, GST has never increased.

"There are no easy paths back to budget sustainability," Aruna Sathanapally, CEO of Grattan Institute and the report's lead author, said.

"But with smarter spending decisions and a tax system that raises sufficient revenue to care for our ageing population, both current and future generations can be better off.

"Reform on this game-changing scale is challenging, but the prize is worth it: a more secure future for Australia's finances, and for all Australians."

A similar 5 per cent increase plan drafted by economist Richard Holden was pitched by Independent MP Kate Chaney in August 2025.

At the time, Holden told SBS News that compared to other "advanced economies", Australia gets about "twice as much of our revenue from income taxes and about half as much of our income from the GST".

At the time, the Greens labelled the plan "lazy", while the Opposition called it "increasingly brave". Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said Labor had not considered a possible GST increase.

"Boosting the GST has become a political no-go zone, in part due to disagreements about how to divvy up the revenue, and concerns it would increase the cost of living," the Grattan Institute report stated.

Where should the revenue go?

The GST increase and expansion will raise about $76 billion a year, according to the Grattan Institute.

The think tank suggests using $58 billion to cut income taxes for low- and middle-income earners and boost welfare payments, which could orchestrate the largest personal income tax cuts in nearly 20 years.

"JobSeeker and Youth Allowance should be raised by 20 per cent, Commonwealth Rent Assistance by 50 per cent, the Parenting Payment by 20 per cent, and pensions by about 8 per cent," the report said.

It suggests allocating the remaining revenue to state governments to shore up their budgets and cut inefficient taxes, such as stamp duty.

It predicts that with the GST increase, most households would pay slightly more in taxes, with larger increases for wealthier and older households.

On the other hand, in estimates, a low-income, single-parent family who rents would be about $150 a week better off, while a higher-income working family would pay $162 a week more in tax.

Would an increase in GST be unfair?

For years, the argument against raising GST was that it would be unfair, particularly to lower-income households.

GST is often described as regressive, in that it takes up a larger share of these households' income than that of higher-income households' income.

This is because higher-income households tend to save more of their income while lower-income households generally spend more of what they earn.

In a July 2025 report, the Australian Council of Social Service argued that increasing the GST to fund income tax cuts "would shift resources from those with the least to those with the most".

However, a recent study by e61–UNSW Policy Research Partnership found that GST may be less regressive than commonly thought. It found households that spend more and those that spend less pay roughly the same share of their spending in GST — about 7.3 per cent.

Examining a household's spending in a year doesn't provide the full picture, the UNSW research partnership says.

Instead, it examined the spending of households across a longer time, taking into account changes in people's circumstances, such as studying, taking parental leave or moving between jobs.

Averaging the years, the gap in GST spending between lower-income and higher-income households narrows.

In other words, the perceived fairness of the GST depends not only on how much people earn, but also on how their spending, saving and longer-term financial position are measured, UNSW says.

The research argues that a reform that includes an increase in GST and paying back the revenue to people "through an unconditional income payment" would be "progressive, irrespective of the measure of household resources".

title: Toxic haze in Southeast Asia worsens amid race to rescue orangutans
text:
In brief Conservation groups are racing to save orangutans in Borneo amid one of Indonesia's worst wildfires.

Pollution levels have risen again and neighbouring countries are badly affected.

Dozens of critically endangered orangutans have been rescued from rampant wildfires burning across Indonesia, as the Borneo residents sue the Indonesian government over negligence in handling the crisis.

The fires have triggered a months-long pollution spell that has closed schools, fuelled a surge in respiratory conditions both among humans and animals, and restricted outdoor activities in Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore and East Timor.

Pollution levels again ranged from unhealthy to very unhealthy across the region on Sunday, cloaking many areas across southern Southeast Asia in toxic haze.

In Indonesia, groups are working to save wildlife from the fires, including orangutans.

On Saturday, the West Kalimantan conservation agency and Indonesian non-profit YIARI said a team evacuated 51 orangutans from locations in the province from 6 August to 19 October.

Figures from Indonesia's forestry ministry suggested this week that the number rescued over recent months in Kalimantan could be as high as 96.

The latest rescue came on Saturday, when three conservation agencies rescued a 20-year-old male orangutan in Indonesia’s island of Borneo.

"The evacuation process was carried out with great caution," the agencies said.

"After the orangutan was sedated, the medical team immediately conducted a health examination before taking the animal to the ... rehabilitation centre," it said.

Indonesia's transport ministry also said around 2,400 flights across the country have been affected by the haze since mid-August.

"Haze reduces visibility around airports, which can lead to delays, disruptions, and even flight cancellations. Every operational decision is made with safety as the top priority," the ministry said.

A group of Indonesians sue the government

Meanwhile, a group of residents on Borneo have sued the government of negligence in handling forest fires that have been raging there for more than three months.

The hearings in the case started this week, the group’s lawyer said on Friday.

It accuses 27 individuals and agencies, including the Indonesian president and vice president, the ministries of forestry and environment, and law enforcement officials and local authorities.

READ MORE Why is the haze so bad in Southeast Asia this year?

Both President Prabowo Subianto and Vice President Gibran Rakabuming Raka have visited areas near the wildfires on Borneo.

Indonesia’s longstanding forest and land fires have worsened this year amid an intensifying El Niño and a prolonged dry season, not only in the Indonesian part of Borneo but also in some regions of Sumatra.

Earlier this week, forest and land fires in Indonesia's Bangka Belitung province in Sumatra spread into a densely populated residential area, damaging at least 300 houses and forcing the evacuation of 500 people.

'Unhealthy' air quality in Singapore

The fire scorched vast expanses of land and has polluted the air as far away as Malaysia and Singapore.

Pollution levels have ranged from unhealthy to very unhealthy across the region on Sunday, cloaking many areas across southern Southeast Asia in toxic haze.

Swiss-based air quality monitor IQAir again ranked Singapore and Kuala Lumpur among the world's five most polluted major cities.

Months of sustained wildfires in Indonesia have blanketed Southeast Asian countries in hazardous haze, with Singapore and Malaysia badly hit. Source: AAP / Then Chih Wey

From 8 am to 9 am local time, the air quality index reached 202, rated "very unhealthy" in Singapore. By noon, it had improved to 163, still in the "unhealthy" range.

At AA Alive, a medical equipment company based just outside of Kuala Lumpur, employees are working at full capacity to deliver oxygen bottles, with officials saying sales were rocketing.

"We have seen a 35 per cent increase in sales because of the haze," Rafina Firdaus, a member of AA Alive's sales team, told AFP during a visit.

"When I started in the industry, I was shocked to see so many patients who need oxygen tanks," she said.

The company supplies patients with both oxygen tanks and oxygen concentrators. An oxygen tank can run for about three hours of continuous use, while a concentrator can be used for about 24 hours.

Md Noor Bin Bujang spent more than a month in hospital and received his first oxygen concentrator on Thursday evening.

He told AFP that without the oxygen-providing equipment he would have "a shortness of breath, especially with the haze".

title: Why is the haze so bad in Southeast Asia this year?
text:
Months of sustained wildfires in Indonesia have caused a spike in respiratory illnesses and blanketed several Southeast Asian countries in hazardous haze, with Singapore and Malaysia also hit badly over the last week.

The pollution has stoked political tensions across the region, with officials questioning Jakarta's handling of the fires as well as its reluctance to accept help from its neighbours.

What is the source of the haze?

The haze is made up of fumes from forest and peatland fires across Indonesia, most notably on the islands of Borneo and Sumatra, which are made up of dense forests and vast stretches of peatland that are especially prone to fire during the dry season, which usually runs from April to October.

The region is also currently under the influence of severe "super-El Niño" weather conditions, which brought additional heat and dryness and caused wildfires to spread more quickly.

The last time Indonesia experienced such intense fires was 2015, when El Niño conditions were similarly severe.

How much damage have the fires done?

Official data on the extent of the land damaged by fire has not been updated since July, when 202,000 hectares had been burned.

But according to environment group Auriga, more than 637,000 hectares were damaged from January to August this year, nine times the area of Singapore.

Deforestation monitor Nusantara Atlas put the figure even higher at nearly 900,000 hectares.

How bad is the haze?

Emissions from Indonesia's fires have been the highest in the world for a month, making up almost half the global total over the last seven days, according to data from Fire Emissions Watch, a portal developed by the European Union's Copernicus climate monitoring service.

Indonesia's air pollution index has shown some areas of Borneo and Sumatra registering pollution levels of over 1,000, with readings of 300 or more already categorised as hazardous.

Singapore's 1-hour PM2.5 reading hit a high of 284 micrograms per cubic metre in the western part of the island state last week, entering the National Environmental Agency's "very high" band for the first time this year.

The number of cases of respiratory illness linked to the fires surged to 283,270 in seven Indonesian provinces alone as of 13 October, more than double the 113,336 reported as of 9 September, the country's health ministry data showed.

Many schools in Indonesia, neighbouring Timor-Leste and some states in Malaysia were forced to close, and nearly 2,000 flights in Indonesia have been affected between 11 August and 12 October.

What is Indonesia doing to tackle the fires?

The Indonesian government says it is doing everything it can.

Over 60,000 personnel have been deployed to fight the fires, and around 50 aircraft have engaged in water bombing and cloud seeding operations.

The government plans to employ more forest rangers to prevent fires, and has vowed to restore its peatland ecosystem, where fires can smoulder underground for much longer and at lower temperatures.

It says it has cracked down on law-breaking enterprises and restricted the use of fire to clear farmland. Police officials have said 223 individuals and nine companies could face action for their involvement in starting forest fires.

Why is Indonesia being criticised?

The Indonesian government has come under increasing international pressure to do more to tackle fires, both before and after they start.

Its crackdown on the use of fire to clear land has not completely eliminated the practice. Rapid deforestation to make way for growing crops, most notably to increase palm oil production, has also raised the risk of fires by draining underground water sources and drying out the soil.

READ MORE Thousands of hectares burnt as El Niño intensifies Indonesia's dry season

The government's reluctance to declare the situation a national disaster, which would allow it to deploy resources more quickly, has also been questioned. It has also not yet accepted offers of help from both Malaysia and Singapore.

How long will the fires and haze last?

Indonesian authorities say that, despite their best efforts, the situation will only be contained when there is sustained rainfall in the region.

The dry season started earlier this year and has lasted longer than usual. Rain usually starts in October, but forecasts say it will be delayed until November.

The effects of El Niño are expected to last until the first quarter of 2027, but the upcoming rain season will help diminish the impact of the fires, Indonesia's weather agency said.

title: Major Woodside gas project paused after Greenpeace protest off Western Australia
text:
The operations at Australian oil and gas giant, Woodside's $12.5 billion Scarborough project in Western Australia have stopped after Greenpeace staged a protest at a floating platform.

On Sunday, the company said it had to pause work at a Scarborough floating production unit off the coast of WA. Two activists from the environmental advocacy group slept overnight on the semi-submersible unit, located about 375 km off the state's northwest coast, in a protest that started on Saturday.

"Temporary hanging tents" were set up on the unit and the activists would "occupy the platform for as long as possible", Greenpeace had said.

The group staged the protest over concerns that Woodside's proposed Browse project's could inflict potential damage to Scott Reef, a remote coral system and foraging area for the endangered pygmy blue whale. Browse and Scarborough are in the same northwest location but more than 1,000 kilometres apart.

Often, question time begins with a few minutes of condolence or bipartisan sentiment. Then it quickly descends into an hour of rancour and abuse that would lose you your job in any other workplace. Members of parliament labelling colleagues “traitors”, calling for them to be “stoned in the square”, to have a bag put over their head, to “rip him a new one”. Politicians are regularly asking our community to disagree well, but our hypocrisy is often on display. Fundamentally, we need to collectively look in the mirror today and consider how it is that we got here. Helen Haines and Allegra Spender in 2022 with their fellow independent MPs Dai Le, Dr Sophie Scamps, Zali Steggall, Zoe Daniel, and Kylea Tink. Alex Ellinghausen Helen Haines is the best of us – a politician with deep roots in her community who brings integrity and intelligence to Canberra. “Minister, I have some serious concerns about this approach. Can you tell me more about ...”

Advertisement

That’s the start of a Helen question. Polite, but extremely effective and probing. Her gentle demeanour belies her enormous contribution, particularly on government accountability and transparency. The people of Indi could not ask for a more diligent, serious and compassionate representative in public life. Related Article Haines attack Independent MP Helen Haines in critical condition after ‘attack’ outside her office Helen is warm and courageous. She will tell you to your face when she doesn’t agree with you, give you good, thought-through reasons, and then follow her conscience. She is funny. She is practical: she laughingly told me that as a bush midwife, she can make a splint out of an old newspaper. When I think of her like this, I am despairing. While Australia does not have a history of political violence, we do have the same trends as other democracies: rising aggression, threats and disruption. Reports of threats and harassment against federal parliamentarians to the Australian Federal Police rose from 279 in 2020-21 to more than 1000 in 2023-24. If you are in parliament, you feel it. You see the threats, the aggression particularly online. You try to ignore them.

Advertisement

What shocks me the most is that almost one in 10 Australians told last year’s McKinnon Index that violence can be justified for a political cause. We are successful as a country because we manage our disagreements through the ballot box, the parliament, the courts, through our institutions. But one in 10 seriously think violence is a political tool. As you look at the statistics, and particularly at online abuse, there is a deeply serious question – how did we get to a place where such aggression is socially permitted? And how do we turn it back? Allegra Spender (left) and Helen Haines (right) at Parliament House in Canberra in August. Dominic Lorrimer None of us have the answer, and we need to be careful about generalising from this specific incident which we still do not understand. But the broader trend of aggression towards politicians needs confronting. Many will point to the security services and their role in keeping politicians safe. That is critical and we need a serious reassessment. But just layering on the security of politicians delivers the opposite of the politics that Helen championed – engaged, available, local – and we mustn’t lose it. Security matters, but our culture I believe matters more and is harder to address.

Advertisement

Social media companies obviously have a role to play. Algorithms amplify outrage because outrage keeps us scrolling, and bots manipulate opinion at scale. ASIO has been clear that online radicalisation is a security risk – from violent Islamist extremism to violent misogyny. Regulation can help, but much of what the social media companies amplify is aggressive content that fellow Australians are putting out there. Editor's pick Haines attack Turn down the temperature: Spy chief’s urgent warning as Helen Haines remains in critical condition When abuse is normalised at the highest level, it makes room not only for extremism but for obsession and derangement. We don’t yet know the perpetrator’s motive or mental state, but Australian and international research shows many people who stalk, threaten or approach politicians live with serious, often untreated, mental illness. Though public discourse rarely makes such a person violent, it can shape who they fixate on and the story they tell themselves about why. It’s not just politicians who are abused and in danger – it’s teachers, nurses, supermarket workers. It’s the sort of abuse our grandmothers would have condemned. Somehow, all of us need to step up and say enough – we treat each other with respect, with dignity. We owe it to each other, whatever we agree or disagree on. No one in public life should ever expect violence. It is most shocking when it is directed at someone who never uses aggression as a political tool.

title: How tech geniuses became Hollywood’s favourite monster
text:
Lions and tigers and tech bros, oh my: Hollywood has a new go-to movie monster in 2026.

From The Social Reckoning to Artificial, today’s on-screen tech bros are more sinister than ever.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

A steely-eyed creature sits in its lair, dark clouds looming in the distance. Several prisoners tentatively enter, gathering the courage to deliver their meagre offerings to the unflinching force before them. The offering doesn’t suffice. With one severe glance, the creature has the prisoners fleeing, desperately hoping they need not return. This sounds like a scene from a horror film – the introduction of Hollywood’s newest flesh-eating beast. But this isn’t your average monster. It’s Mark Zuckerberg, Facebook’s co-founder and Meta chief executive. In Aaron Sorkin’s The Social Reckoning, the tech billionaire is the evil that lurks, the monster under the bed. But instead of a lair, he’s in a sterile office, emotionlessly watching overworked employees present dissatisfying statistics. From The Social Reckoning to Artificial, today’s tech bros appear more monstrous than ever. The film, a follow-up to 2010’s The Social Network (also penned by Sorkin), asks us to reconsider the definition of “monster”, suggesting it’s not fanged creatures and slasher killers we should be afraid of, but rather tech bro billionaires and their unbridled, unchecked power. Set around the 2021 Facebook Files leak, Zuckerberg is no longer the arrogant tech nerd portrayed by Jesse Eisenberg in The Social Network. Now, played by Jeremy Strong (Succession), he’s a robotic, dictatorial techpreneur, intent on increasing Facebook’s engagement even if it means intensifying hate speech, spreading misinformation and damaging mental health. The suggestion of safeguards, which could drop engagement by just one per cent, offends him. When urged to fact-check political ads on the social platform, he refuses, adamant that tech companies shouldn’t operate as arbiters of truth. Facebook, to him, is a corkboard – he can’t control what people pin to it. Jeremy Strong’s Mark Zuckerberg is more “evil lizard man” than arrogant anti-hero. Sony Pictures via AP

Advertisement

Sorkin insists his Zuckerberg is an “anti-hero” rather than a villain, a person with good intentions but poor carry-through. However, Strong’s unfeeling lizard-like performance suggests otherwise. The Social Reckoning is the first of several new movies to turn tech bros monstrous. Andrew Garfield will portray Sam Altman, co-founder of OpenAI, in Luca Guadagnino’s Artificial, landing January 21. Tracking the early development of artificial intelligence, the film’s trailer reads like a psychological horror, as Garfield’s Altman descends into a grim basement filled with guns. “We open Pandora’s Box together, the future is inevitable,” Garfield’s Altman says of AI in the trailer. “Countries will fall, industries are going to collapse, and we get to be the ones to shepherd people into this new world.” Loading It’s difficult to watch without shuddering, knowing that AI has been used to hack into government systems and to mislead using deepfakes and chatbot hallucinations. A former employee from AI safety and research firm Anthropic even warned that AI companies are “gambling with our lives”. Garfield has acknowledged the insidiousness, telling Variety he no longer uses ChatGPT. “I got a bit scared … I felt a little mistrusting of the technology. It feels like the people who are encouraging us to use the technologies don’t exactly know its capacities themselves. That feels a little irresponsible”. Andrew Garfield as Sam Altman and Yura Borisov as Ilya Sutskever in Artificial. Yannis Drakoulidis

Advertisement

Fellow OpenAI co-founder Elon Musk has also attracted Hollywood’s attention. Alex Gibney’s Musk, a nearly four-hour documentary yet to set an Australian release, traces the tech billionaire’s stint in government and ownership of SpaceX, Tesla and X. Musk’s power is so immense that he’s described in the documentary’s teaser trailer as the “Earth’s most unchecked man” and, more concerningly, a “nuke”. Boasting a net worth of nearly $US1 trillion, Musk is the world’s richest person, and with such wealth comes great power. Musk’s lawyers threatened to file a defamation suit ahead of the film’s release, though no suit has officially been filed. Loading Artificial, meanwhile, was dropped by Amazon in June shortly after the company signed a lucrative deal with OpenAI. Coincidence? Luckily, Neon picked it up. Similarly, Sony reportedly received a “strongly worded letter” from Meta after it caught wind of The Social Reckoning. Though these films will land on screens, they’ve had to fight to get there. Perhaps the most anticipated “tech monster” to hit cinemas is Elizabeth Holmes. The disgraced Theranos founder, who’s currently in prison, will be the focus of You Can See Everything, a documentary by Nathan Fielder (The Rehearsal) and Lance Oppenheim (Some Kind of Heaven) landing on November 12. Though only acquitted for defrauding investors, Holmes’ work on the failed blood-testing startup – which provided inaccurate and unreliable blood tests – could have eventually cost lives. Yet in the documentary’s trailer, Holmes insists she did nothing wrong and has “nothing to hide” whilst staring, unblinking, at Fielder, as if trying to consume him with her eyes alone. It’s arguably scarier than any horror film as this is a real person, who has done terrible things for the sake of money and success, and who still fails to acknowledge their ethical shortcomings. Elizabeth Holmes’ stare is beyond unsettling in the trailer for You Can See Everything. YouTube

Advertisement

This is where today’s tech monsters differ from tech bros of the past. Eisenberg’s Mountainhead (2025), a film about four fictional tech tycoons isolating from an economic disaster in a secluded cabin, makes light of their buffoonish behaviour and ineptitude. Jemaine Clement’s tech mogul antagonist in M3GAN 2.0 (2025) is a mash-up of Silicon Valley figures, thus explaining his larger-than-life performance that can hardly be taken seriously. Australian director Leigh Whannell’s The Invisible Man was arguably ahead of the curve in 2020, featuring an exaggeratedly evil tech boss who fakes his suicide and uses a camouflage suit to stalk his ex-partner. Meanwhile, earlier films with real-life tech tycoons, such as The Social Network and Steve Jobs, depicted them more generously. Zuckerberg was a misguided nerd; Jobs was an obsessive genius. Even the fictionalised series about Holmes, The Dropout, showed her dancing to Lil Wayne at one point. They were flawed, but certainly didn’t appear to have the capacity to end the world. Jesse Eisenberg’s Mark Zuckerberg was more twerpy than evil. Sony It seems we can no longer hide behind such levity and fiction. From The Social Reckoning to Artificial, today’s tech bro films are beyond bleak. They capture periods that felt like rock bottom, such as when extremists (many of whom were radicalised on Facebook) stormed the US Capitol. Yet, things have only gotten worse. While earlier films warned of what may come, these films scream: “It’s too late”. That’s scarier than any masked killer or bloodthirsty beast. The Social Reckoning is in cinemas now. I was working with a private client who had a lump-sum of money available to invest. We’d spent some time getting her clarity on her financial position, adding some structure to her finances, and building her understanding of investing. This gave her some assurance, calmed her nerves and improved her confidence in preparation for investing. But the money was still sitting there, in her account – uninvested. Despite all the progress, she felt restless: that task was looming over her head, waiting to be ticked off the checklist. The sky isn’t falling – you can take your time to invest sensibly and strategically. Simon Letch This is something I see in clients a lot: urgency, restlessness, impatience. This feeling of: “I should be further ahead than where I am right now,” or “I’m behind”, or “This is taking too long.” That’s understandable. There is messaging everywhere that reinforces this: from gloom-and-doom headlines that make you lose sleep at night, to the never-ending comparison one can fall into on social media, so no matter how far you get, it never feels like it’s enough.

Advertisement

Many people are convinced this anxiety is helpful. It’s what motivates you to get things done, to achieve and progress. To some extent, that may be true. Editor's pick Opinion

Ask an expert Rich, successful ... now what? How to reignite your financial drive Paridhi Jain Money contributor However, often, this anxiety also pushes people into rushed decisions that just cause more anxiety down the track. For example, you have a lump sum of money you know you “should” invest, but you don’t know how – so you hand it over to the first financial adviser you talk to or buy the first property some family member says to because you just want it off your plate. For a short time, you’re relieved. But quickly, you’re now worried about whether it was the right move. One of the most powerful but underrated skills you can develop on your wealth journey is the ability to tolerate anxiety without reacting to it. Here are some perspective shifts that will help:

Advertisement

Learn to measure progress differently When it comes to money, we are often so anxious to fast-forward to the outcome that we don’t consider anything else progress. We want more money in the bank, we want the house bought, the money invested, the ROI delivered – we want tangible results, and we want them fast. But that’s not how it works. There could be many steps before you arrive at the outcome. Maybe you never had much exposure to the idea of investing until later in your life. Perhaps it took a while for you to overcome your fear of risk. Getting to the finish line isn’t progress – every step towards the finish line is. Maybe you never thought it was even possible for someone without a professional financial background to invest on their own. Maybe you first had to figure out how to stay out of debt and save consistently before investing was an option. Maybe you had to make a few mistakes and lose a bit of money to learn a few lessons.

Advertisement

If you’re impatiently waiting until you finally have $X in investments or $Y net-worth you’re missing (and devaluing) all the progress you’ve made until that point. Getting to the finish line isn’t progress – every step towards the finish line is. Sustainable progress beats fast wins Everyone will sell you fast results – because fast sells. But having now supported hundreds of clients in creating (collectively) millions of dollars of financial outcomes – I can tell you that it’s usually the ones who aren’t trying to rush to the end, who end up growing the fastest long-term. The ones who have achievable goals that they can be excited about. The ones who aren’t measuring progress solely by the number, but by how much they’re learning and growing. The ones who are enjoying the added clarity and confidence that comes with figuring out one more piece of the puzzle – knowing, trusting, that piece by piece, the puzzle will be completed. This is what gives them the ability to stay the course, without getting tired, frustrated, impatient, burnt-out – and ultimately, why they get faster, bigger results, long term.

Advertisement

This takes the ability to enjoy the journey – and not just the outcome. This can be tough when it comes to wealth because – well, of course you just want the outcome, duh. Everyone just wants the money, right? Surely, no one enjoys something as dry and boring as investing, right? Editor's pick Opinion

Collectables Not just nostalgia: Your old toy cars could be a secret goldmine Stephen Crafti Money contributor Listen, I get it. I disliked finance so much in university, I switched my major to economics. But I didn’t have to find enjoyment in the subject itself – I found satisfaction in building my financial confidence, in figuring out something that previously seemed too complex and so on. So, celebrate every milestone; see each step as “one-step-forward” instead of “look-how-far-I-still-have-to-go”; and find satisfaction in your own growth, not just the pot of gold at the end. title: Cirque du Soleil is exuberant old-fashioned circus pleasure, plus other new shows this week
text:
Moore Park Entertainment Quarter, October 18, until January 3.

Roll up – the world’s biggest circus, Cirque du Soleil, is back in town with KOOZA. A throwback to a more interactive, traditional style of circus, KOOZA was created in 2007 by director David Shiner as a departure from the huge theatrical spectacles that had, by then, almost defined Cirque du Soleil’s immensely popular style. Under Shiner’s vision, Stéphane Roy’s set evokes an old-fashioned carnival, and Marie-Chantale Vaillancourt’s costumes are a rainbow of acrobat stripes in nostalgic circus colours.

KOOZA by Cirque du Soleil offers a buffet of spectacular circus skills including contortionists, aerial silks and a devastatingly romantic unicycle duet. Matt Beard & Bernard Letendre

Shiner – a trained clown himself – sent in the clowns. The moment you enter the spiral-patterned big top theatre, it’s hard to spill popcorn without hitting one. Pacing through the audience, the clowns initially favour banter over slapstick, giving the impression that the cast of a North American comedy club has run away with the circus. Once the show begins though, the clowns pull out all the stops with mime, slapstick, and physical theatre.

Kooza features jaw-dropping displays of acrobatic prowess. Matt Beard & Bernard Letendre

While clowns in other Cirque du Soleil shows might have a touch more European arthouse whimsy, these clowns bear the stamp of Shiner’s modern American comedy and vaudeville interests. Their ringleader, Mark Gindick’s slouching, wise-cracking mad King, chants “CHUG, CHUG, CHUG!” as soon as he spies the cans of drink in my and my guest’s hands. He’s accompanied by a bumbling henchman duo (Miguel Berlanga Madroño and Duncan Cameron) straight from a children’s action comedy film. There’s even a fluffy clown-dog who urinates real water.

The Day of the Dead-inspired “Skeleton Dance” has a chorus of skeleton showgirls – just some of the show’s vibrant sets and costumes. Matt Beard & Bernard Letendre

For those requiring a dose of schmaltz, the clowning frames the central narrative: a story about a child-like elfin character known as the Innocent, who arrives complete with kite and upturned red nose just in case you missed the fact he’s meant to represent your inner child.

Performed with great sympathy by Alexandr Yudintsev, the Innocent encounters Mitch Wynter’s dapper Trickster, who prompts him to explore the wider world.

One of the many characters in KOOZA. Matt Beard & Bernard Letendre

Enter the abundant buffet of circus acts the wide-eyed Innocent encounters along the way. There are contortionists, aerial silks, a devastatingly romantic unicycle duet (Anastasiia Shkandybina and Dmytro Dudnyk), an outstandingly charismatic diabolo act (Wei-Liang Lin), a wheel of death scene channelling WWE, and nail-biting highwires and a teeterboard.

All are of Cirque du Soleil’s usual high standard: tightly choreographed, impeccably performed, and eliciting a constant audience rollercoaster of gasps and cheers.

It’s all accompanied by a live band belting out Jean-François Côté’s original music from the top floor of the carnival set. The music and its visual presentation are broad for Cirque du Soleil: following Shiner’s eclectic palette, it spans from the usual ethereal ambient to musical theatre, Bollywood, burlesque, vaudeville, and cabaret. The Day of the Dead-inspired “Skeleton Dance”, featuring Jessica Fox as the Soul Singer, even has a chorus of skeleton showgirls, ostrich feathers bouncing with every strut.

Other commentators have found the clowning excessive, so whether you enjoy KOOZA may come down to personal tastes in comedy style. But with world-class acrobatics and Cirque du Soleil’s extraordinary production values, KOOZA makes an exuberant case for the pleasure of old-fashioned circus.

Chantal Nguyen reviewed a preview performance of KOOZA.

Critical Resources has muscled its way deeper into South America, securing exclusivity over a third gold project in Suriname, just a nine-iron from a monster mine. The company’s new Gadu Manda project sits a mere four kilometres west of Chinese giant Zijin Mining’s Rosebel open pit gold mine, which has churned out more than six million ounces of gold since 2004. The savvy deal boosts the company’s significant ground package in the gold-rich nation to 228 square kilometres, including the new 29-square-kilometre Gadu Manda project, the recently acquired 164-square-kilometre Gonini and its 35-square-kilometre Greenstars gold project. Notably, the company secured exclusive rights over all three on staged low-risk terms in less than a month. Third-party small-scale open pit artisanal workings at Critical Resources’ Gadu Manda project in Suriname, 4km from the giant 6-million-ounce Rosebel gold mine. Under the terms of the latest deal, Critical has entered an exclusivity agreement to acquire a 90 per cent interest in Gadu Manda for a staggered consideration of US$200,000 (A$287,000) in cash over two years and 2.5 million Critical Resources shares, along with a A$287,000 minimum exploration commitment. The arrangement includes a US$10,000 (A$14,326) exclusivity fee, giving the company 60 days to conduct its due diligence. With management already having boots on the ground in Suriname, the company is well placed to fast-track due diligence at Gadu Manda alongside its other recently secured gold projects. Suriname has quietly become a hotspot for global gold capital over the past few years. Precious metal production generated US$2 billion (A$2.87B) in earnings for the nation in 2024 and accounted for almost 80 per cent of its total exports.

Advertisement

‘The project is located about 4km from the pits of Zijin’s Rosebel gold mine, on ground already being worked by small-scale miners.’ Critical Resources managing director Tim Wither That kind of output has not gone unnoticed. The region has seen a flurry of corporate activity of late, led by Zijin’s US$360 million (A$516M) acquisition of the Rosebel mine in 2023. More recently, gold giant Gold Fields tipped C$77 million (A$78.28M) into explorer Founders Metals for a 19.9 per cent stake. At the same time, private investment house La Mancha has taken significant positions in other Canadian-listed explorers active in Suriname. The real sizzle in this deal is the project’s address. Big gold deposits rarely live in isolation. Gadu Manda’s proximity to the Rosebel mine, which boasts a whopping 11.6 million ounces of gold, is the kind of nearology that gets geologists leaping out of bed in the morning. Adding to the intrigue, small-scale artisanal miners have already been working the northern part of the Gadu Manda permit area, with pits and trenches exposing quartz veining. This potentially gives Critical a ready-made set of walk-up targets, with the old-timers having already done the initial sniffing for near-surface gold. All three of Critical’s new projects sit within the Guiana Shield, a well-endowed but relatively underexplored geological province, considered the South American counterpart to West Africa’s phenomenally rich Birimian Shield. While the Birimian belts host more than 500 million ounces of discovered gold, the Guiana Shield lays claim to a still-impressive 100-million-ounce inventory, suggesting there may be plenty of room for new discoveries.

Advertisement

Critical Resources managing director Tim Wither said: “Gadu Manda will be a strong addition to our Suriname portfolio. The Project is located about 4 km from the pits of Zijin’s Rosebel mine, on ground already being worked by small-scale miners. This gives us a head start in developing our understanding of the Project. Together with Gonini and Greenstars, Gadu Manda will give Critical Resources three granted gold projects in a proven gold province. We are currently in Suriname completing due diligence on all three projects, including site visits, while high-level structural targeting work is under way.” The company’s other recently acquired Suriname projects include Gonini,which lies in the historic Sara Creek district within the Marowijne greenstone belt, just 66km from Newmont’s multi-million-ounce Merian gold mine. While gold has been mined in the district for 150 years, the company says there is no record of modern systematic exploration at Gonini. Its second asset, the Greenstars project, sits just 35km west of Zijin’s Rosebel mine. It has road access from the capital, Paramaribo and contains active small-scale alluvial workings, confirming the presence of gold in the local system. Critical says structural targeting by Guiana Shield geophysics specialists GexplOre is now underway across the permits as well as 6000 square kilometres of the surrounding greenstone belt. While the company is clearly making an aggressive push into South American gold, it also holds several other cards in its hand, including the flagship Mavis Lake lithium project in Ontario, Canada, which already holds an 8-million-tonne resource grading 1.07 per cent lithium oxide.

Advertisement

In addition, Critical owns the Halls Peak base metals project in New South Wales, with an inferred resource of 840,000 tonnes at 3.7 per cent zinc and 1.5 per cent lead, and is evaluating next-generation solid-state lithium-ion battery intellectual property in the United States. The company also has interests in a suite of gold, antimony and tungsten prospects in New Zealand, giving it exposure across multiple critical commodities and jurisdictions. For now, however, all eyes are on Suriname. With management on site and a clear strategy to build a significant landholding next door to a world-class mine, Critical appears to have its foot on the accelerator. The company is betting that where there’s smoke, there’s fire – and being just 4km from a 6-million-ounce bonfire seems potentially a very good place to start looking. Many car enthusiasts fondly recall memories of their Holdens and Fords from the 1960s and ’70s. While few held on to these prized automobiles, considerably more still have the model car taking pride-of-place on their shelves, recalling a time when drivers such Peter Brock and Allan Moffat took out titles on the racetrack at Bathurst. These miniature toys, often diecast, still hold memories as well as their value – many toy cars are priced in the hundreds and, occasionally, in the thousands of dollars. A selection of valuable model cars, including a toy Batman car from the ’60s. Jamie Brown, Car Models of Braidwood, Back to Cool For Daniel Parsons, who owns Car Models of Braidwood, a historic township in the Southern Tablelands of NSW, it’s the adults rather than children coming into the store or buying online. “The Holden VF Commodore toy cars are popular. Take the Ford Focus RS WRC08 for $230 or the Chevrolet Camaro for the same amount. It’s a healthy sum given the Chevrolet is a re-release of a 1968 model,” says Parsons.

Advertisement

Some prices of these toy cars can also be attributed to models, such as the Holden and Ford, that are no longer manufactured in Australia. “The saying ‘once they’re gone, they’re gone’ applies to the toys as much as the real thing,” adds Parsons, who sees the choice of toy car as often responding to either the owner’s present car or something they experienced driving as a young adult. Editor's pick Opinion

Collectables Some designer clothing attracts a collector’s premium. But which? Stephen Crafti Money contributor The word “vintage” in the toy world is often used to describe toys only a few decades old. Take a Holden VK Commodore Group C. The winner of the Bathurst 1000 in 1984, driven by Brock, can even be more valuable if the owner has the entire series (each car driven at Bathurst came with a set with numbers emblazoned on the hood and car doors since Bathurst started in 1938) – upwards of $10,000. Peter Neagle, who owns Paul’s Toys in Niddrie, Melbourne, has been surrounded by vintage car toys since his late father, Jack, opened the store in 1953. There are Matchbox cars, Dinky vintage diecast cars as well as Corgi, many from the 1960s through to the ’80s. One of Neagle’s prized cars is his Corgi Batmobile from around 1966, with its fin-like tail lights, with a price estimate of $200 if it comes with its original box. He purchased this from a friend who bought it from a market in Geelong for $120.

Advertisement

“I paid $200, but I estimate this is now worth between $300 and $400.” Those collectors who may have the accompanying Bat Boat could, according to Neagle, be holding something worth an extra $300. Others who prefer to search for their next acquisition online might be tempted by the Corgi Toys NMIB Rov 90 Saloon on eBay for $615. “Prices for certain models can rise quickly if they’re produced in limited quantities,” he adds. Many shops have run dry of vintage car toys. Frank Parker’s shop in Ararat, which he runs with his wife, Denise, has sold most of the vintage toy cars from the 1920s and ’30s. However, he still has a 1970s Monaro, a car that was often raced at Bathurst. Alan Moffat's Mustang. Courtesy Alan Moffat Parker still has a healthy stash of toy cars from the recent past, estimated to be between 4000 and 5000, with about 1000 on display in his shop – many from the 1970s when Moffat and Brock were at their peak, each winning the race several times.

Advertisement

Memories of seeing racing heroes drive at Bathurst, or simply being a young adult behind the wheel of a Holden or Ford, certainly forms an important stimulus in the price paid for toy cars. “I can still recall when my father opened up the world of Corgi diecast cars to me and the Dinky toys, produced in London. It’s not really about the price but the memory of seeing them for the first time and the magic in opening the car doors,” adds Neagle. Critica Limited has kicked the door down with a blockbuster scoping study for its wholly owned Jupiter rare earths project in Western Australia, outlining a potential world-class development sporting a whopping pre-tax net present value (NPV) of $2.67 billion. Using an eight per cent discount rate, the study forecasts a pre-tax internal rate of return (IRR) of 56 per cent. Pre-production capital is estimated at A$555.5 million, with total life-of-mine capital of A$606.2 million, including sustaining and closure costs. Payback is estimated at two years after operations begin. Critica’s Jupiter project in Western Australia’s Mid-West region, 270km from Geraldton. The 14-year operation is projected to generate $12.3 billion in sales revenue and $5.64 billion in pre-tax free cash flow, delivering a hefty average annual return before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation (EBITDA) of A$446 million. The assessment mapped out an eight-million-tonne-a-year conventional open-pit operation, targeting 107.3 million tonnes of ore grading 1879 parts per million (ppm) total rare earth oxides (TREO) over the mine’s life. Indicated mineral resources account for 97 per cent, or 104 million tonnes of the material. Inferred resources account for the remaining 3 per cent.

Advertisement

‘The Jupiter Scoping Study delivers a pre-tax NPV₈ of A$2.7 billion and provides a clear technical foundation for the next phase of development at Jupiter.’ Critica Limited chief executive officer Jacob Deysel Planned output represents just six per cent of Jupiter’s mammoth 1.7-billion-tonne resource, grading 1700ppm TREO, including an initial 160-million-tonne indicated resource. Critica says the remaining 94 per cent lies outside the mine plan, leaving scope for resource conversion and mine-life extensions, subject to further work. Annual production of contained rare earth oxides in mixed rare earth carbonate (MREC) is estimated at 8,300 tonnes, based on an overall recovery of 58 per cent, a grade similar to that achieved in earlier metallurgical testwork. The MREC basket includes neodymium, praseodymium, dysprosium, terbium and yttrium. Using a “beneficiation-first” approach, the processing flowsheet combines magnetic separation and flotation to concentrate the rare earths before sending the upgraded material through the more expensive chemical treatment process, known as hydrometallurgy. Testwork achieved a 14-fold TREO upgrade while rejecting up to 95 per cent of feed mass, massively reducing downstream plant requirements and costs. Critica Limited chief executive officer Jacob Deysel said: “The Jupiter Scoping Study is a major milestone for Critica, demonstrating the potential for a large-scale rare earths development with compelling preliminary economics and a production target overwhelmingly underpinned by Indicated Mineral Resources.”

Advertisement

The model’s base case assumes a gross MREC basket value of US$52.80 (A$81) per kilogram and 75 per cent payability, using an exchange-rate assumption of 65 cents. Adding another layer of financial appeal to Jupiter’s already impressive numbers, Critica’s economic modelling has factored in the Australian Government’s Critical Minerals Production Tax Incentive (CMPTI), a refundable offset of 10 per cent of eligible Australian processing expenditure for up to 10 years. The incentive could deliver up to $264.1 million in benefits, subject to eligibility and qualifying expenditure. Iron, gallium and scandium have no base-case value, leaving them as potential upside. The MREC basket includes neodymium, praseodymium, dysprosium, terbium and yttrium. With the financial foundations now mapped out, Critica has turned its attention to the next development hurdles, pencilling in a prefeasibility study (PFS) from early 2027 to mid-2028, followed by a definitive feasibility study (DFS) through to the end of 2029. Work will include drilling and resource conversion, process optimisation and integrated pilot-plant testing, environmental and heritage studies, product qualification, offtake and partnership discussions, and funding. The development blueprint envisaged construction kicking off in 2030 with first MREC production and sales in 2032. No official reserve has been declared as yet, with Critica keen to emphasise the preliminary study does not guarantee the production target or economic outcomes. The timing of the study is fortuitous, landing as governments seek to diversify rare earth supply chains beyond China. The International Energy Agency says demand for magnet rare earths has doubled since 2015 and is expected to rise by more than 30 per cent by 2030. Australia’s Critical Minerals Strategic Reserve includes rare earths, adding to a more favourable policy backdrop for domestic development.

Advertisement

Critica describes Jupiter as Australia’s largest clay-hosted rare earth resource. It sits 70km south-west of Mount Magnet and 270km east of Geraldton, near road, gas and power infrastructure. Jupiter is one of six rare earth discoveries in Critica’s wholly owned Brothers project, positioning the company to potentially unlock a much bigger district-scale rare earths play. With such robust initial numbers based on just a fraction of Jupiter’s vast resource, Critica has laid out a clear pathway to advance what could become a significant new source of magnet rare earths for Western supply chains. Reigning Open champion Ryan Fox will attempt to become the first Kiwi to win the Australian Open after confirming he will join US Masters champion Rory McIlroy at Kingston Heath in December. It will be the first time the current titleholders of The Open and US Masters have played at the tournament since Gary Player in 1974, while Fox will be aiming to become the first Open champion to win the Australian Open in the same year since Bill Rogers in 1981. New Zealand golfer Ryan Fox holds the Claret Jug as he stands with his wife Anneke Ryff and their two daughters Isabel and Margot during a public reception in Takutai Square. He will get a huge reception at this year’s Australian Open. Getty Images Fox said it was an easy decision to fit the tournament into his schedule, which has become hectic since his dramatic win at Royal Birkdale in July, particularly when the 2026 version is being played at Kingston Heath. Look away now if you are a member at Royal Melbourne. Fox agrees with the controversial view McIlroy expressed ahead of last year’s Australian Open: Kingston Heath is the best sandbelt course.

Advertisement

“My favourite sandbelt course is Kingston Heath,” Fox said from Korea where he is preparing to play this week. Although keen not to upset anyone too much ahead of his return to the country where he learned to play the tough, uncompromising and sometimes brilliant golf which prevailed at The Open, he said rating one course above the other was splitting hairs. View post on X But his preference was clear. “I am definitely in Rory’s boat. I think my favourite is Kingston Heath on the sandbelt, but it is not like they are miles apart. You give me a chance to play either and I am very excited to play,” Fox said.

Advertisement

“It is just a personal thing. I just like the feel of Kingston Heath and the look of some of the shots. I have been lucky enough to play both in tournament conditions. [The chance to play] either of them I am not complaining. “They are some of the best courses anywhere in the world but for me Kingston Heath’s just got it by a hair basically.” Ryan Fox will bring the famous Claret Jug with him to Australia to play at Kingston Heath in December. Warren Little Fox said the automatic admission Australian Open winners were granted into the US Masters and The Open had increased the incentive for the world’s best players to play in the tournament. But he said it was not the only reason the best players in the world were considering making an Australian summer part of their schedule. He said the momentum was real. “If you look at who has won the Stonehaven cup, it’s pretty impressive. It’s the who’s who of golf, [and] it’s an event guys really, really want to play,” Fox said.

Advertisement

Fox finished equal 14th alongside McIlroy in last year’s Open won by Denmark’s Rasmus Neergaard-Petersen after being the joint leader at the end of the opening day. He said his major victory had helped him feel as though he belongs among the sport’s big names and playing in the high-profile groups. On the course, Fox has handled the expectation with comes with his new-found status, but he admitted he was battling to manage his time as effectively as he would like when it came to the increased expectations off the course. One of the most down-to-earth and likeable players on the tour, Fox said he had sought the advice of US Open champion Geoff Ogilvy during the President’s Cup. “He said it does calm down a bit, but the cool thing is it kind of never leaves you as well,” Fox said. “You will always be a major champion. There will always be a bit of extra buzz around.”

Fox said he has to get better at saying no to certain demands now that his downtime was not as free as it once was. He said he was looking forward to going on a fishing trip when the chance arose. He will arrive in Australia, knowing he has the claret jug, but also the game and mental resilience to contend in any tournament. “[I know I] can deal with pressure. title: Twin brothers win Lotto twice in two years
text:
Twin brothers have defied the odds and are planning to hit the road after they celebrated their second lotto win within two years.

The Albany brothers, 65, from Western Australia's Great Southern, shared a $1m Millionaire Medley prize within two years of winning Set For Life.

The first win helped them buy their sister's home, now they can pay off the property and hit the road.

Both winning tickets were purchased from Clark's Newsagency in Albany.

The Albany brothers, 65, from Western Australia's Great Southern, shared a $1m Millionaire Medley prize within two years of winning Set For Life.

One of the lucky brothers said he bought the ticket after his dentist appointment was cancelled.

"When I got home, I realised I'd bought a Slikpik and forgotten to get my usual numbers as well," he said.

"I wouldn't usually ever buy more than one ticket a day, but when I realised I'd only bought the Slikpik, I thought I'd pop back because I like playing the same numbers.

"I know it's completely random, but it's what I like to do."

The second trip to the retailer resulted in a System 8 entry that secured the $1 million prize.

"We're set now," one brother said.

"We've worked physically demanding jobs our whole lives but now we can relax a bit more, pay the house off and then we both want to get caravans so we can travel around Australia together."

The twin brothers have won Lotto twice within two years.

While one brother is dreaming of life on the road, the other has already celebrated in his own way.

"I bought myself a watch because you have to treat yourself a bit," he said.

"I also like disco and dancing, so I might celebrate with my girlfriend."

"Winning a major prize is a memorable moment for any player, but to experience two significant wins within such a short period is remarkable," she said.

"It's wonderful to see these brothers using their prizes to secure their future and enjoy retirement together."
